measurementObjective: Given data and a described sorting method, give the arrangement after one or two passes.
distractorStrategy: The fully sorted result given where one pass was asked; a pass applied in the wrong direction; the largest item placed at the wrong end. The fully-sorted distractor catches students who know the outcome and not the process.
notes: Method described in words in the stem; no algorithm names required.

conceptName: How much work an operation costs
factStatement: Some operations take the same work whatever the size, and others take more as the data grows.
familyName: Comparing how two operations scale
measurementObjective: Given two operations, say which does more work as the data grows and why.
distractorStrategy: Reading a position assumed to cost more for a longer array; inserting at the end confused with inserting at the front; both assumed equal because both are one line of code. The last is the real misconception.
notes: In words and counts, never notation.

factStatement: Accessing a position that does not exist either fails or gives meaningless data, depending on the language.
familyName: Reasoning about an access past the end
measurementObjective: Say what happens when a traversal reads one position too far.
distractorStrategy: The access assumed always to fail loudly; assumed to return an empty value; assumed to wrap to the start. Loop bounds written with the length rather than length-minus-one is the natural stem.
notes: Complements CC_FAM09 from the algorithm side rather than the language side.

factStatement: Some problems are solved by moving two positions toward each other rather than by traversing twice.
familyName: Tracing two positions moving through data
measurementObjective: Given data and a described two-position method, say what the positions hold after several steps.
distractorStrategy: One position moved and not the other; the crossing condition applied one step late; the values swapped where only the positions moved. Reversing in place is the clearest stem.

factStatement: Whether the data is sorted, and how large it is, decides which approach is appropriate.
familyName: Choosing a search or traversal approach
measurementObjective: Given a stated requirement and the shape of the data, choose the appropriate approach.
distractorStrategy: A halving search on unsorted data; sorting first where one lookup is needed; a single traversal where every pair must be compared. The stated shape of the data must decide it.

factStatement: A result that is one item short, or misses the first or last item, points to a specific bound or starting-value fault.
familyName: Diagnosing an off-by-one from the result
measurementObjective: Given a traversal and a result that is wrong in a stated way, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: A fault that would miss the other end; a fault that would give a different kind of wrongness; the data blamed rather than the bounds. The specific way it is wrong must implicate one fault.
notes: A maximum initialised to zero over all-negative data is the strongest D5 stem.

factStatement: Empty and single-item data break approaches that assume at least two items.
familyName: Behaviour on empty or single-item data
measurementObjective: Say what a described approach produces for empty or single-item data.
distractorStrategy: The ordinary-data answer; a failure where a wrong value is returned quietly; a value where it genuinely fails. Comparing adjacent pairs on a single item is the canonical case.

conceptName: How much work an operation costs
factStatement: Making one operation cheaper usually makes another dearer, so the right structure depends on what will be done most.
familyName: Judging a trade-off between operations
measurementObjective: Given the operations a program performs most, choose the arrangement of data that suits it.
distractorStrategy: Keeping data sorted where insertions dominate; leaving it unsorted where lookups dominate; a choice that ignores the stated usage. The usage pattern must decide, and both options must be workable.

factStatement: Text is a sequence of characters at numbered positions, including spaces and punctuation.
familyName: Reading a character at a position
measurementObjective: Given text, name the character at a position or the position of a character.
distractorStrategy: Spaces not counted as characters — the essential case; one-based positions; punctuation skipped. Text with a space in the middle must appear.

factStatement: The length counts every character, including spaces.
familyName: Counting the length of text
measurementObjective: Give the length of stated text.
distractorStrategy: Spaces omitted; words counted instead of characters; a trailing space missed. Use text where the difference is one or two, so careless counting shows.

factStatement: Two pieces of text differing only in case are not equal unless case is deliberately ignored.
familyName: Deciding whether two pieces of text match
measurementObjective: Say whether two pieces of text compare equal.
distractorStrategy: Case assumed ignored; a leading space assumed ignored; the comparison assumed to fail on length alone. Options must preserve case exactly — the case IS the content.
notes: Nothing downstream may compare these options case-insensitively.

factStatement: Taking a range of characters uses a start and an end, and whether the end is included is a fixed rule.
familyName: Working out what a range produces
measurementObjective: Give the text a stated range produces.
distractorStrategy: The end included when it is not; one character short at the start; the range read backwards. Off-by-one at each end is the whole family.

factStatement: Operations on text produce a new value and leave the original unchanged.
familyName: What the original holds after an operation
measurementObjective: Say what the original variable holds after an operation on it.
distractorStrategy: The original assumed modified in place — the central misconception; the result assumed discarded; both assumed to change. Requires an operation whose result is not assigned back.

factStatement: Searching text gives the position of the first match, or an indication that there is none.
familyName: What a search within text returns
measurementObjective: Give the result of searching for stated text, including when it is absent.
distractorStrategy: The last match returned rather than the first; a not-found result treated as position zero — the bug that makes absent text look present; the count of matches returned.
notes: The not-found-as-zero confusion is worth several items.

factStatement: Splitting text produces pieces determined by where the separator occurs, including empty pieces.
familyName: How many pieces splitting produces
measurementObjective: Given text and a separator, say how many pieces result and what they are.
distractorStrategy: Empty pieces from consecutive separators omitted; a leading or trailing separator ignored; the separator included in the pieces. Consecutive separators are the D4 case.

factStatement: Joining pieces places the separator between them, so there is one fewer separator than pieces.
familyName: What joining produces
measurementObjective: Give the text produced by joining stated pieces.
distractorStrategy: A separator added at the end; one fewer separator than needed; the pieces concatenated with no separator. The counting relationship is the measurement.

factStatement: Leading and trailing spaces are part of the text and change comparisons and lengths.
familyName: Reasoning about invisible characters
measurementObjective: Say why two pieces of text that look identical do not match.
distractorStrategy: The mismatch attributed to case where the cause is a space; to length where both are the same length; assumed impossible because they look the same. The stem must make the space visible in the description.
notes: The single most common cause of "but they are the same" in real input handling.

factStatement: Traversing text one character at a time can count occurrences or build new text.
familyName: What a character-by-character traversal produces
measurementObjective: Give the count or the text a described traversal produces.
distractorStrategy: Spaces included where they should be skipped and the reverse; the count off by one at an end; the built text in the wrong order. Counting vowels in text with a space is a good stem.

factStatement: Whether text reads the same backwards is decided by comparing characters from both ends.
familyName: Reasoning about a symmetry check
measurementObjective: Say whether stated text passes a described symmetry check, and how many comparisons it takes.
distractorStrategy: A check that ignores case where the stem says it should not; one that includes spaces where it should not; the comparison count given as the full length rather than half. Case and spaces must be specified in the stem.

conceptName: How much work text operations cost
factStatement: Building text by repeatedly adding to it does more work than assembling the pieces once.
familyName: Comparing the cost of two ways of building text
measurementObjective: Given two ways of building the same text, say which does more work and why.
distractorStrategy: The two assumed equivalent because the result is the same; the cost attributed to the number of lines of code; the cheaper method identified with the wrong reason. The reason must be that each addition copies.
notes: Depends on DS_FAM05: it costs more precisely because the original is never modified.

factStatement: Output missing its first or last character, or with a stray separator, points to a specific range or loop fault.
familyName: Diagnosing a text fault from the output
measurementObjective: Given text output that is wrong in a stated way, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: A fault that would break the other end; a fault producing a different kind of wrongness; the input blamed. A trailing separator and a missing last character must be distinguishable from the output alone.

factStatement: Empty text and single-character text break approaches that assume at least two characters.
familyName: Behaviour on empty or single-character text
measurementObjective: Say what a described approach produces for empty or single-character text.
distractorStrategy: The ordinary answer; a failure where an empty result is returned quietly; a result where it genuinely fails. A symmetry check on empty text, which is trivially symmetric, is the sharpest case.

factStatement: Splitting, traversing and searching each suit different text tasks.
familyName: Choosing how to process text
measurementObjective: Given a text task, choose the approach that handles it, including its awkward inputs.
distractorStrategy: An approach that works on tidy input and fails on repeated separators; one that needs several passes where one suffices; one that solves a slightly different task. The awkward input must be stated.

factStatement: A table holds rows of the same shape, where each column holds one kind of value.
familyName: Identifying rows, columns and values
measurementObjective: Given a table in the stem, name a row, a column or a value.
distractorStrategy: A row named as a column; the header counted as a row; a column described as holding mixed kinds of value.

factStatement: A key is a column whose value identifies exactly one row and is never repeated.
familyName: Recognising which column could be a key
measurementObjective: Given a table, identify which column can serve as a key.
distractorStrategy: A column that happens to be unique in the sample but is not unique in principle — a name, a date of birth; a column with a repeat visible in the data; a column with a missing value. The name column is the essential distractor.
notes: The sample data must contain the counterexample.

factStatement: Each column holds one type of value, which decides how it can be compared and sorted.
familyName: Recognising the type a column should hold
measurementObjective: Given a column of sample values, say what type it should be.
distractorStrategy: A phone number typed as a number, which loses leading zeros — the productive case; a date stored as text; a yes/no stored as free text.

factStatement: The same fact stored in several rows can be updated in one and not the others, leaving the data contradicting itself.
familyName: Reasoning about what duplication causes
measurementObjective: Given a table with repeated data, say what goes wrong when one copy is changed.
distractorStrategy: Duplication described as merely wasteful — true but not the point; described as harmless because the values match today; the problem attributed to size rather than to consistency.
notes: The reason tables get split, and therefore the reason relationships exist.

factStatement: A column holding another table's key links a row to a row in that table.
familyName: Following a link between two tables
measurementObjective: Given two tables, say which row in one a stated row in the other refers to.
distractorStrategy: The link followed in the wrong direction; matched on a name column rather than the key; a row with no matching reference assumed to match the first. Show both tables.

factStatement: A relationship may allow one match or many, and which it is decides where the reference is stored.
familyName: Deciding whether a relationship is one-to-many
measurementObjective: Given a described situation, say how many rows on each side may correspond.
distractorStrategy: A one-to-many relationship read the wrong way round; a many-to-many treated as one-to-many; the reference placed on the side that would need repeating. The direction is the measurement.

factStatement: Moving a repeated fact into its own table leaves each fact recorded once.
familyName: Deciding what to move into its own table
measurementObjective: Given a table with repeated data, choose the split that records each fact once.
distractorStrategy: A split on a column that is not actually repeated; one that leaves the duplication in place; one that splits so far that a simple question needs three tables. Cost of over-splitting is the D4 case.
notes: Normalisation reasoning without the vocabulary or the numbered forms.

factStatement: A missing value is not the same as zero or as empty text, and comparisons against it do not behave normally.
familyName: Reasoning about a missing value
measurementObjective: Say how a missing value behaves in a comparison or a total.
distractorStrategy: Missing treated as zero in a total; treated as equal to another missing value; treated as matching an "is not" condition. All three are wrong for the same underlying reason.
notes: Foundation-critical: it silently changes counts and averages.

factStatement: A constraint refuses data that would break a rule, at the moment it is written.
familyName: Reasoning about what a constraint prevents
measurementObjective: Given constraints and an attempted insertion, say whether it is accepted.
distractorStrategy: A duplicate key accepted; a reference to a non-existent row accepted; a missing value accepted where the column requires one. Each must be decidable from the stated constraints.

factStatement: Rows are not stored in a guaranteed order; any order you rely on must be asked for.
familyName: Reasoning about the order rows come back in
measurementObjective: Say whether a described result is guaranteed to be in a particular order.
distractorStrategy: Insertion order assumed guaranteed; key order assumed guaranteed; the order seen once assumed stable. This is why "the first row" is not a well-defined idea.

factStatement: Answering a question that spans tables means matching rows on the linking column.
familyName: Working out the rows a combination produces
measurementObjective: Given two small tables, say how many rows the described combination yields.
distractorStrategy: The sum of the two row counts; the product, which is what happens with no matching condition; unmatched rows counted as though matched. The unmatched-row case is the important one.
notes: Prepares SQ_FAM11 without requiring SQL syntax.

factStatement: A count or total that is wrong usually comes from duplication, missing values, or an unmatched link.
familyName: Diagnosing a wrong count or total
measurementObjective: Given data and a wrong result, identify which of the three causes explains it.
distractorStrategy: Duplication blamed where a missing value is the cause; a missing value blamed where a row failed to match; the calculation blamed rather than the data. The data must distinguish them.

factStatement: A design choice made now decides which questions are easy and which become impossible to answer accurately.
familyName: Judging a design by the questions it permits
measurementObjective: Given a design and a question to be answered later, say whether the design can answer it.
distractorStrategy: A design that stores a computed total and so cannot answer about its parts; one that stores several values in one column; one that is fine. Storing "history" only as a current value is the strongest D5 case.
notes: The most transferable idea in the skill: a design forecloses questions.

factStatement: Empty tables and rows with no match are where a query or a report gives a misleading answer.
familyName: Reasoning about empty or unmatched data
measurementObjective: Say what a described report shows when a table is empty or rows do not match.
distractorStrategy: An error assumed where a zero or an empty result is returned; a total of zero presented as reliable; unmatched rows assumed included. Averaging over an empty result is the canonical case.

factStatement: Choosing a real-world value as a key ties the data to something that can change.
familyName: Judging a choice of key
measurementObjective: Given candidate keys, choose the one that stays valid and say what breaks with the others.
distractorStrategy: An email address, a phone number or a name chosen as a key — each unique today and mutable tomorrow. The consequence must be stated, not just the choice.

factStatement: A query names the columns it wants back, and every matching row supplies them.
familyName: What columns a query returns
measurementObjective: Given a table and a query, say which columns come back.
distractorStrategy: All columns returned where two were named; the rows filtered when no condition was given; the column order assumed to follow the table rather than the query.
notes: Show the table and the query in the stem throughout this skill.

factStatement: The clauses of a query must appear in a fixed order, whatever order they are thought of in.
familyName: Recognising a correctly ordered query
measurementObjective: Identify which of several queries is written in a valid order.
distractorStrategy: Filtering placed after ordering; grouping placed before filtering; ordering placed before the table is named. The one syntax family admitted, because a wrong order stops the query running at all.
notes: The only deliberate syntax family in the skill.

factStatement: A condition keeps the rows that satisfy it and discards the rest.
familyName: How many rows a condition keeps
measurementObjective: Given a table and a condition, say how many rows come back.
distractorStrategy: A boundary row included or excluded wrongly; the count of columns given; rows with a missing value in the tested column assumed to match. Include a boundary value in the data.

factStatement: Conditions joined by and must both hold; joined by or, either suffices.
familyName: How many rows a combined condition keeps
measurementObjective: Given a table and a combined condition, say which rows come back.
distractorStrategy: and and or swapped; a negation applied to only the first condition; the rows satisfying either given for an and. Data must distinguish all four cases.

factStatement: Rows come back in a defined order only when one is asked for, and ties are not broken by anything unstated.
familyName: The order rows come back in
measurementObjective: Given data and an ordering, give the sequence of rows.
distractorStrategy: Descending read as ascending; ties assumed to keep insertion order; ordering assumed to apply before filtering. Include tied values.
notes: Depends on DB_FAM10.

factStatement: A summary function turns many rows into one value.
familyName: What a summary function returns
measurementObjective: Given a table, give the count, total or average a query returns.
distractorStrategy: Rows with a missing value counted in an average — the D4 case, since it changes the divisor; the count of all rows given where a column was counted; the total given where the average was asked. Data must include a missing value.
notes: Depends on DB_FAM08 and is where that fact earns its place.

factStatement: Grouping produces one summary row per distinct value of the grouping column.
familyName: How many rows a grouped query returns
measurementObjective: Given data and a grouped query, say how many rows come back and what each holds.
distractorStrategy: One row returned in total; one row per original row; the number of groups counted wrongly because a value repeats. The result must be countable from the shown data.

factStatement: Filtering rows before grouping and filtering groups afterwards give different answers.
familyName: Deciding where a filter belongs
measurementObjective: Given a requirement, say whether the condition applies to rows or to groups.
distractorStrategy: A group condition placed on rows; a row condition placed on groups; both assumed interchangeable. A requirement mentioning a count is a group condition and must be recognised as such.

factStatement: A query returns repeated values unless duplicates are explicitly removed.
familyName: Reasoning about repeated values in a result
measurementObjective: Given data, say how many rows come back with and without duplicate removal.
distractorStrategy: Duplicates assumed removed automatically; removal assumed to apply per column rather than per row; the count of distinct values given where all rows were asked for.

factStatement: A row whose tested column is missing satisfies neither a condition nor its negation.
familyName: Reasoning about missing values in a condition
measurementObjective: Given data with missing values, say which rows a condition returns.
distractorStrategy: Missing rows returned by the negated condition — the case that surprises everybody; missing treated as zero; missing treated as matching everything. The row counts must not add up naively, which is the lesson.
notes: The strongest family in the skill for exposing a wrong mental model.

factStatement: Combining tables matches rows on a linking column, and rows without a match are left out unless asked for.
familyName: How many rows a two-table query returns
measurementObjective: Given two small tables, give the number of rows a combined query returns.
distractorStrategy: The sum of the row counts; the product, which is what happens with no matching condition; unmatched rows counted as included. Both tables must contain an unmatched row.
notes: Depends on DB_FAM11.

factStatement: A question stated in words determines what the query must select, filter and group.
familyName: Choosing the query that answers a question
measurementObjective: Given a question in words and several queries, choose the one that answers it exactly.
distractorStrategy: A query answering a nearby question; one correct but returning extra columns; one whose filter is off at the boundary. All must be valid queries, so the reasoning is about meaning.

factStatement: Too many rows, too few, or a wrong total each point to a specific fault in the query.
familyName: Diagnosing a query from its wrong result
measurementObjective: Given a query and a result that is wrong in a stated way, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: A missing match condition, which multiplies rows; a filter at the wrong stage, which changes a total; a missing value, which changes an average. Each produces a different wrongness and the stem must say which.
notes: A missing match condition producing a row explosion is the canonical D5 stem.

factStatement: A query matching nothing returns an empty result, and a summary over nothing is not zero for every function.
familyName: Reasoning about a query that matches nothing
measurementObjective: Say what a summary query returns when no rows match.
distractorStrategy: An error assumed; every summary assumed to return zero, when a count does and an average does not; no rows assumed to mean no result row at all. The count/average difference is the measurement.

factStatement: Two queries can return the same rows for this data and differ for other data.
familyName: Judging whether two queries always agree
measurementObjective: Decide whether two queries always return the same result, and describe data that separates them.
distractorStrategy: A pair differing only when a value is missing; a pair differing only when a row is unmatched; a genuinely equivalent pair. Reasoning beyond the shown data is the measurement.

factStatement: A network carries data between machines that each have an address.
familyName: Recognising what a network provides
measurementObjective: Identify what is needed for two machines to exchange data.
distractorStrategy: A network described as the internet; as requiring a browser; as needing both machines switched on at the same instant for any exchange. Complements HCW_FAM11 at a technical level.

factStatement: A machine is reached by an address; a name is a convenience that must be turned into one.
familyName: Distinguishing a name from an address
measurementObjective: Say which of a name and an address the network uses to route data.
distractorStrategy: The name assumed to be used directly; the address assumed to be the same thing as the name; one name assumed to mean one machine forever.

factStatement: A port distinguishes different services on the same machine.
familyName: Recognising what a port distinguishes
measurementObjective: Say what a port identifies and what happens when two services want the same one.
distractorStrategy: A port assumed to identify a machine; assumed to be a physical socket; two services assumed able to share one. This is exactly the local-development confusion a first-year hits.

conceptName: Turning a name into an address
factStatement: Before a request can be sent, the name must be looked up to find the address.
familyName: Ordering lookup and request
measurementObjective: Put the steps of reaching a named machine in order.
distractorStrategy: The request assumed sent to the name directly; lookup assumed to happen after connecting; lookup assumed to happen once for all sites.

factStatement: An address that means "this machine" or "this network" cannot be reached from elsewhere.
familyName: Reasoning about who can reach an address
measurementObjective: Say whether a described machine can be reached from another network.
distractorStrategy: A local address assumed shareable — the "it works on my machine" belief; a same-network address assumed reachable from the internet; a public address assumed private.
notes: The first genuinely useful networking fact for someone running a local server.

factStatement: Data is split into pieces that travel separately and are reassembled on arrival.
familyName: Reasoning about data arriving in pieces
measurementObjective: Say what can happen to the pieces in transit and what the receiver must do.
distractorStrategy: Data assumed to travel as one unit; pieces assumed to arrive in order always; a lost piece assumed to lose everything. Out-of-order arrival is the productive case.

factStatement: One kind of transport checks that everything arrived and in order; another does not, and is faster for it.
familyName: Reasoning about guaranteed against fast delivery
measurementObjective: Given a use, say which kind of delivery suits it and what is given up.
distractorStrategy: Guaranteed delivery chosen for live video, where lateness is worse than loss; unguaranteed chosen for a file transfer; the choice justified by speed alone with no mention of loss. No protocol names required.

factStatement: Data crosses several machines on the way, none of which is the destination.
familyName: Reasoning about the path data takes
measurementObjective: Say what the machines along the path do and do not do.
distractorStrategy: A direct connection assumed; intermediaries assumed to read or store the content; the path assumed identical in both directions. The last is a genuine and useful surprise.

factStatement: Addressing, delivery and the meaning of the data are separate responsibilities.
familyName: Assigning a responsibility to a layer
measurementObjective: Given a described job, say which layer of responsibility it belongs to.
distractorStrategy: Retransmission attributed to addressing; the meaning of the content attributed to delivery; encryption attributed to routing. Responsibilities in words, never a numbered model to recite.
notes: Deliberately not a layer-model recall family; builds on HCW_FAM13 on abstraction.

factStatement: Capacity is shared, so one heavy user affects others, and distance adds delay independently of capacity.
familyName: Distinguishing capacity from delay
measurementObjective: Given a symptom, say whether capacity or delay explains it.
distractorStrategy: More capacity offered as the fix for a delay problem — the commonest real confusion; delay blamed for a slow large download; both treated as one quantity called speed.

conceptName: Turning a name into an address
factStatement: A lookup result is remembered for a time, so a changed address is not seen immediately.
familyName: Reasoning about a remembered lookup
measurementObjective: Say what happens after a name is pointed at a new address.
distractorStrategy: The change assumed instant everywhere; assumed never to propagate; the browser cache blamed rather than the lookup. Complements BR_FAM06 at a different layer.

factStatement: Traffic can be blocked by port or by destination, at either end or anywhere between.
familyName: Reasoning about where traffic was blocked
measurementObjective: Given that a connection fails from one place and works from another, say where the block is.
distractorStrategy: The server blamed where the client network blocks; the name lookup blamed where the port is closed; the application blamed. The "works for me" asymmetry is the evidence.

factStatement: A failure to resolve, to connect, or to get a reply are different symptoms pointing to different stages.
familyName: Locating the stage a connection failed at
measurementObjective: Given the symptom, identify which stage failed and what to check.
distractorStrategy: A name failure diagnosed as a server fault; a closed port diagnosed as a name failure; a slow reply diagnosed as a failure. D5 gives a case where the name resolves and nothing answers, which has two plausible causes separated by one detail.
notes: The most practically useful family in the skill.

factStatement: Anything crossing a network unencrypted can be read by whoever handles it on the way.
familyName: Judging who can see what crosses a network
measurementObjective: Given a described situation, decide what a party on the path can learn.
distractorStrategy: Encryption assumed to hide which site was contacted; a private network assumed to make traffic unreadable; a password assumed safe because the page looked private. Extends HP_FAM10 to the network path.

factStatement: Making a local service reachable from elsewhere requires a reachable address and an open path to its port.
familyName: Reasoning about what makes a service reachable
measurementObjective: Given a service that works locally and not remotely, choose what must change.
distractorStrategy: Sharing the local address; changing the port with no path opened; assuming a public name is sufficient without a reachable address. Every option must be something a student would actually try.
notes: Genuine transfer: it requires CN_FAM05, CN_FAM03 and CN_FAM12 together.

factStatement: A claim about all members of a group says something different from a claim about some of them.
familyName: Recognising how much a claim asserts
measurementObjective: Given a statement, say whether it is about all, some, or none of a group.
distractorStrategy: A some-claim read as an all-claim — the error behind most invalid inferences; a none-claim read as a some-not claim; a claim about a subset read as about the whole.

factStatement: The denial of "all are" is "at least one is not", not "none are".
familyName: Choosing the denial of a claim
measurementObjective: Given a claim, choose the statement that denies it exactly.
distractorStrategy: "None are" offered as the denial of "all are" — the classic over-negation; the original claim restated; a stronger claim than the denial requires.

factStatement: Two groups may overlap entirely, partly, or not at all, and a statement usually does not settle which.
familyName: Recognising what an overlap statement fixes
measurementObjective: Given two groups and a statement relating them, say what is settled about their overlap.
distractorStrategy: A partial overlap read as total; "some A are B" read as implying some A are not B; disjointness assumed where nothing said so.

factStatement: A conclusion either follows from the statements given or it does not; nothing outside them may be used.
familyName: Deciding whether a one-step conclusion follows
measurementObjective: Given one or two statements, say whether a stated conclusion follows.
distractorStrategy: A conclusion that is true in the world but does not follow — the essential distractor; one that follows from a reversed statement; one requiring an extra unstated fact.
notes: Real-world truth must be irrelevant, and at least one distractor should be plainly true and still invalid.

factStatement: Membership passes along a chain of all-claims but not along some-claims.
familyName: Following membership through a chain
measurementObjective: Given a chain of group statements, say what follows about a named member.
distractorStrategy: A chain of some-claims treated as transitive — the commonest failure; the chain followed backwards; a conclusion about the wrong group.

factStatement: Two statements together may support a conclusion neither supports alone.
familyName: Combining two statements
measurementObjective: Given two statements, choose the conclusion they jointly support.
distractorStrategy: A conclusion following from one statement alone; one requiring a third; one that reverses the direction of the second. All must be about the right subject.

factStatement: An invalid step has a recognisable shape — reversing a conditional, treating some as all, concluding from a single case.
familyName: Finding the step that does not follow
measurementObjective: Given a short argument, identify the step that is not warranted.
distractorStrategy: Steps that are valid; a step that is valid but uninteresting; the conclusion blamed rather than the step. Exactly one step must be unwarranted, and the argument must reach a plausible conclusion.
notes: A plausible conclusion from invalid reasoning is the point — otherwise students answer from the conclusion.

factStatement: From "if A then B" and B, nothing follows about A; from "if A then B" and not-B, it follows that not-A.
familyName: Reasoning in the right direction from a conditional
measurementObjective: Given a conditional and one further fact, say what follows.
distractorStrategy: The converse asserted — affirming the consequent, the most common error in the whole skill; the inverse asserted; "nothing follows" chosen where something does.
notes: Include cases where the honest answer IS "nothing follows".

factStatement: A set of ordering constraints may fix a position, rule some out, or leave several possible.
familyName: Deducing a position from ordering constraints
measurementObjective: Given constraints on an order, say what is fixed about a named item.
distractorStrategy: A position consistent with some constraints and not all; a position fixed by an assumption nobody stated; "cannot be determined" where the constraints do fix it. Keep to four or five items so it stays reasoning rather than bookkeeping.

factStatement: Items grouped together share a property, and stating that property is what identifies the odd one.
familyName: Stating the rule behind a grouping
measurementObjective: Given a group of items and one that does not belong, state the property that separates them.
distractorStrategy: A property shared by all including the odd one; a property that separates a different item; a property true of the group but not the discriminating one. Asking for the RULE rather than the odd item is what stops a lucky guess.
notes: Items must be computing or everyday, never obscure general knowledge.

factStatement: A proposed arrangement either satisfies every constraint or violates a specific one.
familyName: Testing an arrangement against constraints
measurementObjective: Given constraints and a proposed arrangement, say whether it holds and which constraint fails.
distractorStrategy: An arrangement violating exactly one constraint, offered as valid; the wrong constraint named as violated; an arrangement rejected for breaking a constraint that was never stated.
notes: Same fact family as AL_FAM09; testing rather than deducing.

factStatement: A condition that guarantees an outcome need not be the only way to reach it.
familyName: Distinguishing what guarantees from what is required
measurementObjective: Given a stated condition, say whether it is enough, required, both, or neither.
distractorStrategy: Sufficient treated as necessary and the reverse; both claimed where only one holds; neither claimed where one holds. The distinction is invisible to students and shapes how they read every requirement later.

conceptName: What an argument takes for granted
factStatement: An argument can require something it never states, and it fails if that thing is false.
familyName: Finding what an argument assumes
measurementObjective: Identify the unstated thing an argument needs in order to work.
distractorStrategy: A stated premise offered as the assumption; a true fact the argument does not need; a restatement of the conclusion. Distinguishing "needed" from "merely true" is the measurement.
notes: Same shape as PS_FAM05 but about arguments rather than solutions; different skill, so a separate group by rule.

conceptName: What an argument takes for granted
factStatement: The evidence given may support a modest conclusion while not supporting a stronger one.
familyName: Choosing the strongest warranted conclusion
measurementObjective: Given evidence, choose the strongest conclusion it actually supports.
distractorStrategy: A conclusion one step too strong — the whole measurement; one so weak it is uninformative; one about a subject the evidence does not cover. Several options must be true and only one maximally warranted.

factStatement: A new fact can weaken an argument by undermining what it assumed, without contradicting its conclusion.
familyName: Choosing what would weaken an argument
measurementObjective: Given an argument, choose the fact that most undermines it.
distractorStrategy: A fact that contradicts the conclusion directly rather than weakening the reasoning; one irrelevant to the assumption; one that strengthens it. Attacking the assumption rather than the conclusion is the insight.

factStatement: Consecutive terms differ by a step, which may be constant or itself change.
familyName: Continuing a constant-step series
measurementObjective: Give the next term of a series whose step is constant.
distractorStrategy: The step applied once too many or too few times; the step taken from the wrong pair; the step applied in the wrong direction for a decreasing series.

factStatement: The rule of a series can be stated, not merely continued.
familyName: Naming the step of a series
measurementObjective: Given a series, state the rule relating each term to the previous one.
distractorStrategy: A rule fitting the first pair only; an additive rule for a multiplicative series; a rule that fits every term but is needlessly complicated. Naming rather than continuing removes the guess.

factStatement: An analogy asserts that one pair stands in the same relation as another.
familyName: Naming the relation in a pair
measurementObjective: Given a pair of terms, state the relation between them.
distractorStrategy: A relation that holds in the reverse direction; one true of both terms separately but not between them; a category relation where the real one is functional. Computing pairs — compiler and source, file and folder — keep it out of general knowledge.

factStatement: The step itself can follow a rule, so the differences form their own series.
familyName: Continuing a series whose step changes
measurementObjective: Give the next term where the differences form a pattern.
distractorStrategy: The last difference reused as though constant; the difference-of-differences applied as the step; the step pattern continued but added to the wrong term.

factStatement: Completing an analogy means applying the same relation, not finding a similar word.
familyName: Completing an analogy
measurementObjective: Given three terms, choose the fourth that preserves the relation.
distractorStrategy: A term merely associated with the third; one preserving the relation reversed; one from the same category as the third but unrelated by the relation. Association is the trap.

conceptName: More than one rule at once
factStatement: A series may interleave two patterns, each governing every other term.
familyName: Continuing an interleaved series
measurementObjective: Give the next term of a series with two interleaved patterns.
distractorStrategy: A single rule fitted to consecutive terms; the wrong one of the two patterns continued; the right pattern continued from the wrong term. Interleaved series look chaotic under a single-rule assumption, which is what is being probed.

factStatement: A gap in the middle of a series is fixed by the terms on either side of it.
familyName: Filling a gap in the middle
measurementObjective: Give the missing term from a series with an internal gap.
distractorStrategy: A term consistent with the left side and not the right; one consistent with both only if the rule changed; the term that would come next rather than the one missing. Both sides must be needed.
notes: Stronger than a next-term item, because a rule inferred from one side alone fails.

factStatement: A series may grow by a factor rather than a difference, and the two look alike early on.
familyName: Continuing a multiplicative series
measurementObjective: Give the next term where each is a multiple of the previous.
distractorStrategy: The additive continuation, which agrees for the first two terms — the essential distractor; the factor applied twice; the factor read from the wrong pair. Early terms must be consistent with both readings.

factStatement: A series of letters or symbols can be governed by position rather than by value.
familyName: Continuing a positional series
measurementObjective: Give the next item in a letter or symbol series.
distractorStrategy: The step counted off by one in the alphabet; the wrap-around handled wrongly; a value pattern applied where the rule is positional. Write the series as plain characters so no image is needed.

conceptName: More than one rule at once
factStatement: Two things about each term may change independently, each with its own rule.
familyName: Continuing a series with two varying attributes
measurementObjective: Give the next term where two attributes each follow their own rule.
distractorStrategy: One attribute continued correctly and the other frozen; both continued with the same rule; the attributes swapped. Every option must get at least one attribute right.

factStatement: A proposed rule must account for every term given, not merely the first few.
familyName: Choosing the rule that fits every term
measurementObjective: Given a series, choose the rule consistent with all of it.
distractorStrategy: A rule fitting all but the last term — the distractor that catches students who stop checking; one fitting every term but predicting a different next; one fitting only the extremes.

conceptName: A term that does not fit
factStatement: A series may contain exactly one term inconsistent with the rule the rest follow.
familyName: Finding the term that breaks the rule
measurementObjective: Given a series with one wrong term, identify it and say what it should be.
distractorStrategy: A term that would be wrong under a different rule; the term after the break rather than the break; the last term, which students suspect by default. The rule must be inferable from the remaining terms alone.

conceptName: When more than one rule fits
factStatement: Given terms can be consistent with more than one rule, which then disagree about what comes next.
familyName: Reasoning when two rules both fit
measurementObjective: Given a series that two rules both fit, say what further term would distinguish them.
distractorStrategy: A term consistent with both rules and therefore useless; one inconsistent with both; one that distinguishes a third rule nobody proposed. Choosing the discriminating term is the same reasoning as PS test selection, in a different setting.
notes: One of the few genuinely deep families in an aptitude skill.

factStatement: A rule inferred from one series can be applied to a different starting point.
familyName: Applying an inferred rule to a new start
measurementObjective: Infer the rule from one series and apply it to a different first term.
distractorStrategy: The original series continued instead; the rule applied to the wrong starting term; a rule that fits the original by coincidence and does not generalise. Genuine transfer, because the answer is not in the series shown.

conceptName: When more than one rule fits
factStatement: Two terms are consistent with infinitely many rules, so the next term is not determined.
familyName: Recognising when a series is undetermined
measurementObjective: Say whether the terms given fix the next one, and why not if they do not.
distractorStrategy: The simplest rule offered as the answer — which is exactly the assumption being examined; a rule that fits and is not unique; a claim that no rule fits at all. Include series that ARE determined, or the family teaches that nothing ever is.
notes: Intellectually the most honest family here, and the one most series questions quietly get wrong.

factStatement: A value in a table is located by its row and its column together.
familyName: Reading a value from a table
measurementObjective: Given a table in the stem, read the value at a stated row and column.
distractorStrategy: The adjacent row or column read; a total read as a value; the transposed cell. Show a small table so the answer is checkable.

factStatement: A number means nothing without its unit and scale — thousands, percentages, per month.
familyName: Reading a value with its unit and scale
measurementObjective: Given data with a stated scale, give the actual quantity.
distractorStrategy: The raw number given without applying the scale — the commonest careless error; the scale applied twice; a monthly figure read as annual.
notes: The scale must be stated in the table header and must matter.

factStatement: A chart shows values by position or length, and reading it means recovering the numbers.
familyName: Reading values from a described chart
measurementObjective: Given a chart described in text, identify the largest, smallest or a named value.
distractorStrategy: The second largest given; a category confused with its neighbour; a cumulative value read as a single one. Descriptions must be unambiguous, since no image can be shown.
notes: Charts are described in prose or as value lists; the skill is the arithmetic reasoning, not visual estimation.

factStatement: Totals and differences are computed from the data and are not themselves data.
familyName: Computing a total or a difference
measurementObjective: Give the total across a row or the difference between two values.
distractorStrategy: A total including a subtotal already counted — the essential trap; a difference taken in the wrong direction; one value omitted. The table must contain a subtotal row.

factStatement: A share depends on which total it is taken against.
familyName: Computing a share of the right whole
measurementObjective: Give a value as a proportion of a stated total.
distractorStrategy: The share taken against the wrong total — a row total instead of the grand total; the reciprocal; the share of a different category. The table must offer more than one plausible whole.

factStatement: A percentage change is measured against the earlier value, so the same absolute change is a different percentage from a different base.
familyName: Computing a percentage change
measurementObjective: Give the percentage change between two values.
distractorStrategy: The change taken against the later value; the absolute difference given as a percentage; a rise of 50 then a fall of 50 assumed to return to the start. The last is the D4 case and the most instructive.

factStatement: A ratio compares two quantities and says nothing about their absolute size.
familyName: Reasoning from a ratio
measurementObjective: Given a ratio and one quantity, give the other, or compare two ratios.
distractorStrategy: A ratio treated as a share of the whole; the two parts added where the total was given as one part; a larger ratio assumed to mean a larger absolute quantity. The last is the D4 measurement.

factStatement: An average is consistent with very different distributions, and adding a value moves it toward that value.
familyName: Reasoning about what an average does and does not say
measurementObjective: Say what follows from a stated average, and how a new value changes it.
distractorStrategy: The average assumed to be a typical value; assumed to be a value in the data; two averages of different-sized groups averaged directly — the D4 case, and a genuine trap.

factStatement: A trend describes the direction of change and does not fix any individual value.
familyName: Reading a trend correctly
measurementObjective: Given a series of values, say what the trend is and what it does not tell you.
distractorStrategy: A rising trend read as every value rising — the essential distractor, requiring one dip in the data; a trend extrapolated as a prediction; the largest single jump read as the trend.
notes: The data must rise overall while falling somewhere.

factStatement: A per-unit figure depends on what it is divided by, so comparing rates means checking the denominators match.
familyName: Comparing two rates
measurementObjective: Given two rates, say whether they are comparable and which is larger.
distractorStrategy: Rates with different denominators compared directly; a count compared with a rate; the larger count assumed to be the larger rate. A small group with a high rate is the sharpest stem.

factStatement: Successive percentage changes multiply rather than add, and a percentage of a percentage is not their sum.
familyName: Reasoning about successive percentage changes
measurementObjective: Give the overall effect of two successive percentage changes.
distractorStrategy: The two percentages added; the second applied to the original base; the order assumed to change the result when it does not. Adding is what nearly everybody does.
notes: Same fact family as AD_FAM06, one level up.

factStatement: Missing entries, mismatched totals and changed definitions make a figure unreliable.
familyName: Spotting a problem in the data itself
measurementObjective: Given a table, identify what makes a stated figure unreliable.
distractorStrategy: A cosmetic issue offered as a data problem; a genuine problem in a column the question does not use; the arithmetic blamed where the data is at fault. The table must contain the defect visibly.
notes: Ties to DB_FAM08 on missing values, in a different setting.

factStatement: A truncated scale, a relative figure without its base, or a selected period can mislead while every number is correct.
familyName: Identifying how a correct figure misleads
measurementObjective: Given a described presentation, say what makes it misleading.
distractorStrategy: An accusation that a number is wrong when all are right; a stylistic objection; a real problem in a part of the presentation the claim does not rest on. "A 200% rise" from two cases to six is the canonical stem.
notes: The most valuable family in the skill and the most transferable outside it.

factStatement: A question may require a figure the data does not contain, and no arithmetic recovers it.
familyName: Deciding whether the data answers the question
measurementObjective: Say whether the data given is sufficient, and what would be needed if not.
distractorStrategy: A plausible number derivable only by assuming something unstated; a figure from a related row; the answer to a nearby question the data does support. Some variants must be answerable, or the family teaches that nothing ever is.

factStatement: A claim can go beyond what the data shows — asserting a cause, a future value, or a group not measured.
familyName: Judging whether the data supports a claim
measurementObjective: Given data and a claim, say whether the data supports it and where it overreaches.
distractorStrategy: A claim of cause from a correlation; a claim about a group not in the data; a prediction from a short series. Every claim must be consistent with the data and only one fully supported by it.

factStatement: A repeating pattern is built from a unit that recurs, and identifying the unit describes the whole.
familyName: Identifying the repeating unit
measurementObjective: Given a symbol sequence, identify the shortest unit that repeats.
distractorStrategy: A unit twice the length of the true one — it repeats, but is not shortest; a unit that fits the start and not the rest; a single symbol where the unit is longer. Asking for the shortest is what makes one answer correct.
notes: Sequences are written as plain characters; no image is required anywhere in this skill.

factStatement: A symmetric arrangement maps onto itself, with each element matching a partner.
familyName: Recognising whether an arrangement is symmetric
measurementObjective: Given a written arrangement, say whether it is symmetric and about what.
distractorStrategy: An arrangement symmetric except at one position; one symmetric about a different axis than claimed; a repeating sequence mistaken for a symmetric one. Repetition and symmetry are genuinely different and confused.

factStatement: Turning, mirroring and shifting are different operations with different results.
familyName: Naming the transformation applied
measurementObjective: Given a before and after arrangement, name the transformation.
distractorStrategy: A mirror and a half-turn confused — they agree on symmetric input, which is why the input must not be symmetric; a shift called a turn; two transformations named where one suffices.
notes: The input must be asymmetric or two transformations become indistinguishable.

factStatement: Once the repeating unit is known, the element at any position follows from its place in the cycle.
familyName: Predicting the element at a position
measurementObjective: Give the element at a stated position in a repeating sequence.
distractorStrategy: The element one position out from counting from one instead of zero; the element at the position within the unit rather than the sequence; the last element of the unit. Positions beyond what is shown force reasoning rather than counting.
notes: Ask about a position well past the shown sequence.

factStatement: Items can share a structure while sharing none of their content.
familyName: Finding the item with a different structure
measurementObjective: Given several arrangements, identify the one whose structure differs.
distractorStrategy: An item differing in content while sharing the structure — the essential distractor; one differing in length only; one differing by a transformation that preserves structure. Content must vary throughout so it cannot be the discriminator.
notes: Distinct from AS analogies: this is about structure, not relation between a pair.

factStatement: Turning an arrangement by a stated amount produces exactly one result.
familyName: Predicting the result of a turn
measurementObjective: Given a grid described by coordinates and a stated turn, give the resulting arrangement.
distractorStrategy: A turn in the wrong direction; a mirror instead of a turn; a turn of the wrong amount. Describe the grid as occupied coordinates so the answer is unambiguous.
notes: Small grids — two by two or three by three — described as coordinate lists.

factStatement: Mirroring depends on the axis, and mirroring twice about the same axis restores the original.
familyName: Predicting the result of mirroring
measurementObjective: Give the result of mirroring an arrangement about a stated axis, or of doing so twice.
distractorStrategy: The wrong axis used; a turn substituted; a double mirror assumed to differ from the original. The double-mirror case is the D4 measurement.

factStatement: A sequence of moves on a grid has a combined effect that can be worked out without following each step.
familyName: Tracking a position through several moves
measurementObjective: Give the final position after a stated sequence of moves.
distractorStrategy: One move omitted; a direction reversed; the moves summed without regard to a turn that changed the facing. Turning as well as moving is the D4 case.

factStatement: A pattern can contain a smaller pattern, each with its own rule.
familyName: Reading a pattern inside a pattern
measurementObjective: Given a nested arrangement, say what comes next at the level asked about.
distractorStrategy: The outer pattern continued where the inner was asked and the reverse; both continued with one rule; the inner rule applied at the wrong point in the outer cycle.

factStatement: The structure several items share can be stated as a rule independent of their content.
familyName: Stating the structure items share
measurementObjective: Given several items, state the structural rule they all satisfy.
distractorStrategy: A rule true of the content rather than the structure; a rule fitting all but one; a rule fitting all but more specific than the items support. Abstraction, not observation, is the measurement.

factStatement: Several attributes of an item can each follow their own rule at the same time.
familyName: Continuing a pattern with several attributes
measurementObjective: Given items varying in two or three attributes, give the next.
distractorStrategy: One attribute continued correctly and another frozen; all attributes given the same rule; two attributes swapped. Every option must be right about at least one attribute.
notes: Attributes stated in words — shape, count, orientation — never shown.

factStatement: A growing arrangement adds a predictable number of elements at each stage.
familyName: Counting the elements at a later stage
measurementObjective: Give the number of elements in a stated stage of a growing pattern.
distractorStrategy: The count from continuing by the last increment rather than the rule; the stage number confused with the count; the count for the previous stage. Ask about a stage far enough out that listing is impractical.
notes: Overlaps AS series but is about a structure being built, not a numeric sequence.

factStatement: An arrangement that mostly follows a rule breaks it at an identifiable place.
familyName: Locating where a pattern breaks
measurementObjective: Given an arrangement with one deviation, identify where it occurs and what should be there.
distractorStrategy: The position after the break; a position that deviates under a different candidate rule; the end of the sequence. The rule must be inferable from the unbroken part alone.

factStatement: A structure recognised in one setting can be recognised in an entirely different one.
familyName: Recognising the same structure in a new setting
measurementObjective: Given a structure in one form, identify the item sharing it in a different form.
distractorStrategy: An item in the same form as the original but a different structure; one in a different form with a superficially similar look; one sharing the structure partly. Content must differ completely, so only structure can decide.
notes: The point of the whole skill: abstraction is what makes it transferable to programming.

factStatement: An arrangement can be consistent with two different structures that predict different continuations.
familyName: Reasoning when two structures both fit
measurementObjective: Given an arrangement fitting two structures, say what would distinguish them.
distractorStrategy: A continuation consistent with both and therefore uninformative; one consistent with neither; a claim that only one structure fits. Same discriminating-evidence reasoning as AS_FAM13 and PS_FAM15.

factStatement: A technical term means one thing, and using it loosely changes what a sentence claims.
familyName: Reading a technical term correctly
measurementObjective: Given a sentence using a technical term, say what it asserts.
distractorStrategy: The everyday sense of the word substituted for the technical one — memory, process, argument, exception are all worth using; a related term's meaning; a plausible but wider claim than the term supports.
notes: Terms must come from the Foundation curriculum so the item measures reading, not vocabulary a student has never met.

factStatement: Each instruction applies to something specific and in a specific place in the sequence.
familyName: Reading what an instruction applies to
measurementObjective: Given a numbered procedure, say what a stated step acts on.
distractorStrategy: The step applied to the result of a later step; applied to the whole rather than the named part; the step read as optional. The procedure must be short and unambiguous.

factStatement: A message reports, requests, asks, or decides, and its purpose determines what it must contain.
familyName: Identifying what a message is trying to do
measurementObjective: Given a short message, identify its purpose.
distractorStrategy: A report read as a request — the confusion that leaves nobody knowing whether action is needed; a question read as a statement; an opinion read as a decision.

factStatement: Following a procedure exactly produces one outcome, whatever was intended.
familyName: Working out what following the steps produces
measurementObjective: Given a procedure and a starting state, say what results from following it literally.
distractorStrategy: The intended outcome rather than the literal one — the whole point; the outcome with a step skipped; the outcome with the steps reordered sensibly. A procedure whose literal reading differs from its intent is required.
notes: Directly parallel to HCW_FAM03: the machine does what you said, not what you meant.

factStatement: A passage states some things, implies others, and leaves the rest unaddressed.
familyName: Answering from a technical passage
measurementObjective: Given a short passage, answer a question it does address.
distractorStrategy: A true statement the passage does not make; a claim from a different part of the passage; a plausible inference the passage rules out. Distinguishing stated from merely true is the measurement.

conceptName: Wording that can be read two ways
factStatement: An instruction that can be followed in two different ways contains an identifiable ambiguity.
familyName: Finding the instruction that could be read two ways
measurementObjective: Given several instructions, identify the one that permits two different actions, and say what the two are.
distractorStrategy: An instruction that is merely terse but unambiguous; one ambiguous in a way that does not change the action; one whose ambiguity is resolved by an earlier step. Naming BOTH readings is what makes this verifiable rather than a matter of taste.
notes: This framing is why the whole skill is measurable in multiple choice: the answer is checkable from the text.

factStatement: A problem report is only actionable if it says what was expected, what happened, and how to reproduce it.
familyName: Identifying what a report fails to say
measurementObjective: Given a bug report, identify the missing piece that prevents anyone acting on it.
distractorStrategy: Information that is present; information that would be nice but is not blocking; information the reader could reasonably infer. Exactly one omission must genuinely prevent action.
notes: Pairs with DG_FAM04: the report is unactionable precisely because it cannot be reproduced.

factStatement: A message assumes its reader knows certain things, and fails if they do not.
familyName: Identifying what a message assumes its reader knows
measurementObjective: Given a message and a stated reader, identify what the reader would not understand.
distractorStrategy: A term the stated reader would certainly know; one they would not need; a stylistic objection. The reader must be described specifically, so the answer is derivable rather than a judgement.
notes: Specifying the reader is what turns an opinion question into a measurable one.

conceptName: Wording that can be read two ways
factStatement: Of two phrasings describing the same thing, one may admit fewer readings.
familyName: Choosing the phrasing that admits one reading
measurementObjective: Given phrasings of the same requirement, choose the one that cannot be misread.
distractorStrategy: A phrasing that is shorter but ambiguous; one longer and still ambiguous; one precise about the wrong thing. "At least" against "more than" and "up to" against "under" are the productive pairs.
notes: Connects directly to CB_FAM11: the boundary word decides the condition.

factStatement: A document has parts with distinct jobs, and information put in the wrong part is not found.
familyName: Deciding which part information belongs in
measurementObjective: Given a document structure and a piece of information, say where it belongs.
distractorStrategy: Setup instructions placed under usage; a known limitation buried in the description; a prerequisite stated after the steps that need it. The reader's path through the document must decide it.

factStatement: A question can only be answered if it states what was tried, what happened, and what was expected.
familyName: Deciding which request can be answered
measurementObjective: Given several help requests, identify the one that can be answered as written.
distractorStrategy: A polite request with no detail; a detailed request that never states what was expected; a request containing everything except what was tried. Answerability, not politeness, is the criterion.

factStatement: Feedback is useful only if the recipient can tell what to change.
familyName: Deciding which feedback can be acted on
measurementObjective: Given several comments on the same work, identify the one that says what to change.
distractorStrategy: A judgement with no direction; a direction with no reason; a comment about the person rather than the work. All must be civil, so tone cannot be the discriminator.
notes: Keeping every option civil is what stops this becoming a politeness question.

factStatement: When a reader does the wrong thing, the words that permitted it can usually be identified.
familyName: Locating the words that caused a misunderstanding
measurementObjective: Given instructions and what the reader actually did, identify the wording responsible.
distractorStrategy: Wording that is imperfect but not what misled; the reader blamed rather than the text; a step that is genuinely clear. The reader's action must be a reasonable reading of exactly one phrase.
notes: The strongest family in the skill: the reader's behaviour is the evidence, so the answer is verifiable.

factStatement: A specific defect in wording has a repair that addresses it, and other improvements do not.
familyName: Choosing the rewrite that fixes the stated defect
measurementObjective: Given a message with a named defect, choose the rewrite that removes it.
distractorStrategy: A rewrite that improves something else and leaves the defect; one that removes the defect and introduces another; one that is shorter and equally ambiguous. Naming the defect in the stem is what makes one rewrite correct.
notes: Without a named defect this would be a taste question. With one, it is checkable.

factStatement: Whether something needs a written record, an immediate reply, or a shared document follows from what it is for.
familyName: Choosing the form a message needs
measurementObjective: Given a situation with stated constraints, choose the form of communication that satisfies them.
distractorStrategy: A form that fails a stated constraint — no record where one is required, no immediacy where it is; one that satisfies the constraints and reaches the wrong people; one that would work if a stated constraint did not exist. The constraints must decide it.
notes: Constraints stated explicitly, or this becomes preference.

factStatement: An explanation says why something happens; a description says only what it is.
familyName: Telling an explanation from a description
measurementObjective: Given several statements, identify the one that explains rather than describes.
distractorStrategy: A restatement of the behaviour offered as its cause — circularity is the essential distractor; a definition; a correct but unrelated mechanism.

factStatement: An analogy claims a correspondence between parts of two things.
familyName: Identifying what an analogy maps to what
measurementObjective: Given an analogy, say which part of the technical thing a stated part corresponds to.
distractorStrategy: A correspondence to the wrong component; a mapping that reverses the direction; a part of the analogy with no counterpart. Familiar analogies — memory as a desk, a queue as a line — keep it about the mapping.

conceptName: Words the reader may not have
factStatement: A word is jargon when the reader does not have it, not because of the word itself.
familyName: Identifying which term the reader lacks
measurementObjective: Given an explanation and a described reader, identify the term that would stop them.
distractorStrategy: A term the described reader would certainly know; a long word that is not technical; a term explained earlier in the passage. The reader must be described specifically.

factStatement: An explanation must establish what a later step depends on before that step.
familyName: Ordering an explanation so each step is supported
measurementObjective: Given the parts of an explanation, choose the order in which nothing depends on something unsaid.
distractorStrategy: An order using a term before defining it — the checkable defect; one that is chronological but not logical; one that starts with the conclusion and never supports it. Dependency, not style, decides.

factStatement: An explanation can be easy to follow and still be factually wrong.
familyName: Finding the false step in a clear explanation
measurementObjective: Given a fluent explanation, identify the step that is not true.
distractorStrategy: Steps that are true; a step that is true but simplified; the conclusion, which follows from the false step. The explanation must read well, so fluency cannot be the cue.
notes: Facts drawn from earlier Foundation skills so correctness is decidable.

factStatement: An explanation is incomplete if the step it leaves out is the one that answers the question.
familyName: Identifying the step an explanation leaves out
measurementObjective: Given an explanation and the question it was answering, identify the missing step.
distractorStrategy: A detail that is missing and irrelevant to the question; a step that is present; extra depth that would not help. The question asked must decide what counts as missing.

factStatement: An analogy holds up to a point and then predicts something false.
familyName: Finding where an analogy stops being true
measurementObjective: Given an analogy, identify the conclusion it would wrongly support.
distractorStrategy: A conclusion the analogy supports correctly; one it says nothing about; one false for a reason unrelated to the analogy. Knowing where an analogy breaks is what separates using one from being misled by it.
notes: A checkable question with one right answer, which is why analogy is measurable here at all.

conceptName: Words the reader may not have
factStatement: An explanation can fail by being too shallow to answer the question or too deep to be followed.
familyName: Judging whether the depth suits the question
measurementObjective: Given a question, a reader and an explanation, say whether the depth is wrong and how.
distractorStrategy: An explanation that is accurate and does not answer what was asked; one that answers it and assumes unavailable knowledge; one that is correct at the right depth. Both the question and the reader are stated, so the answer is derivable.

factStatement: Restating the symptom, or naming something that merely accompanies it, is not an explanation.
familyName: Distinguishing a cause from a restatement
measurementObjective: Given several accounts of why something happens, identify the one naming a cause.
distractorStrategy: The symptom restated in technical words — the commonest fake explanation; a correlate offered as a cause; a cause one level too far back to be useful. Circularity must be plausible-sounding.
notes: Pairs with DG_FAM14 on root cause, from the explaining side.

factStatement: An example helps only if the thing being explained is what makes it work.
familyName: Choosing an example that illustrates the point
measurementObjective: Given a concept, choose the example that demonstrates it.
distractorStrategy: An example of a neighbouring concept; a correct example so complex the point is buried; an example where the concept is present but incidental. Each must be a true example of something.

factStatement: A simplification is acceptable when what it omits does not change what the reader will conclude.
familyName: Judging whether a simplification misleads
measurementObjective: Given a simplified explanation, say whether it leaves the reader with a false belief.
distractorStrategy: A simplification that omits detail harmlessly; one that omits detail and creates a false prediction; one that adds a falsehood outright. The distinction between harmless and harmful omission is the measurement.
notes: Directly relevant to teaching: this is the judgement a tutor makes constantly.

factStatement: Explaining a technical choice means giving the reason it was preferred, not restating what was chosen.
familyName: Choosing the account that justifies a decision
measurementObjective: Given a decision, choose the account that explains why it was made.
distractorStrategy: A restatement of the decision; an appeal to convention with no reason; a reason that would equally support the rejected option. The last is the sharpest.

factStatement: Correcting someone means addressing the belief they hold, not merely stating the right answer.
familyName: Choosing the response that corrects the belief
measurementObjective: Given a stated misconception, choose the response that would change it.
distractorStrategy: A correct statement that does not engage the belief; one that contradicts it without explaining why it seemed right; one addressing a different misconception. Misconceptions drawn from earlier batches — the CPU stores files, a loop always runs once.
notes: The most valuable family here, and the one that reuses the distractor work from every other skill.

factStatement: A specific fault in an explanation has a repair that addresses it and others that do not.
familyName: Choosing the fix for a stated fault
measurementObjective: Given an explanation with a named fault, choose the change that fixes it.
distractorStrategy: A change that improves clarity and leaves the fault; one that fixes the fault and introduces an inaccuracy; one that adds detail nobody needed. The fault must be named in the stem.

factStatement: An explanation that works for one reader must be rebuilt, not merely shortened, for a different one.
familyName: Re-explaining for a different reader
measurementObjective: Given an explanation for one reader, choose the version that works for a different stated reader.
distractorStrategy: The original shortened, which keeps the assumed knowledge; one that removes the jargon and the substance with it; one that replaces jargon with an analogy that misleads. Both readers must be described specifically.

factStatement: Different roles spend their time on different work, whatever their titles suggest.
familyName: Matching described work to a role
measurementObjective: Given a description of daily work, identify the role.
distractorStrategy: A role whose title sounds closer than its work; a role sharing some of the tasks; a role that would do it in a small team only. Descriptions must be concrete tasks, not adjectives.
notes: Roles limited to those a first-year will actually encounter.

factStatement: A CV asserts, a portfolio demonstrates, and a reference vouches; they do different jobs.
familyName: Recognising what each artefact does
measurementObjective: Given a need, identify which artefact addresses it.
distractorStrategy: A CV treated as evidence rather than as a claim — the distinction the whole skill rests on; a portfolio treated as a list; a reference treated as a formality.

factStatement: An internship, a graduate role and an experienced role expect different evidence.
familyName: Recognising what a route expects
measurementObjective: Given a route of entry, identify what it expects a candidate to show.
distractorStrategy: Experience expected of an internship; nothing expected of a graduate role; a qualification treated as sufficient on its own.

factStatement: A role depends on specific skills, and skills outside them do not substitute.
familyName: Identifying the skills a role rests on
measurementObjective: Given a role, identify which of several skills it depends on most.
distractorStrategy: A skill useful in every role and therefore not discriminating; a skill from an adjacent role; a tool named where the underlying skill is what matters. Tool-against-skill is the productive confusion.
notes: Skills drawn from the Foundation taxonomy so the link is real.

factStatement: A claim becomes evidence when someone else can verify it independently.
familyName: Distinguishing evidence from assertion
measurementObjective: Given several statements about a candidate, identify which is verifiable.
distractorStrategy: A confident self-assessment; a course completed with no output; a claim about effort rather than result. Verifiability, not impressiveness, is the criterion, and that is what makes the item checkable.
notes: The framing that keeps this skill measurable rather than a matter of career opinion.

factStatement: A project is evidence of the particular skills it required, not of skills it merely touched.
familyName: Identifying what a project actually demonstrates
measurementObjective: Given a described project, say which claimed skill it supports.
