distractorStrategy: A skill the project used trivially; one implied by the topic but not exercised; one the project would demonstrate if a stated part had not been supplied ready-made. The last is the D4 measurement.
notes: A tutorial followed step by step demonstrates following instructions, and that must be recognisable.

factStatement: A stated skill is supported only if something else in the document demonstrates it.
familyName: Finding the claim nothing supports
measurementObjective: Given a CV extract, identify the claim nothing else in it evidences.
distractorStrategy: A claim supported by a listed project; one supported by a stated outcome; one modest and supported. Exactly one claim must be unsupported by anything present, and the extract must be short enough to check.

factStatement: Roles with overlapping work differ in what they are accountable for.
familyName: Distinguishing two similar roles
measurementObjective: Given two adjacent roles, identify what separates them.
distractorStrategy: A difference of seniority offered as a difference of role; a difference in tools; a difference true at one employer only. Accountability, not title, is the discriminator.

factStatement: Whether an opportunity is worth taking depends on the goal it is meant to serve.
familyName: Judging an opportunity against a stated goal
measurementObjective: Given a goal and an opportunity, say whether it advances the goal and how.
distractorStrategy: An opportunity attractive on other grounds; one advancing a different goal; one that would advance the goal if a stated constraint did not rule it out. The goal must be stated, or this is opinion.

factStatement: Some career steps depend on something being in place first, so the order matters.
familyName: Reasoning about what must come first
measurementObjective: Given several intended steps, identify which depends on another being done first.
distractorStrategy: Two steps that are genuinely independent claimed as dependent; a dependency in the wrong direction; a preference presented as a prerequisite. Only real dependencies count — applying for something requires having the thing it asks for.
notes: Kept to logical dependency rather than advice about what year to do what.

factStatement: The gap to a role is what it requires minus what can currently be demonstrated.
familyName: Identifying the gap to a stated role
measurementObjective: Given a role and a candidate's evidence, identify the largest gap.
distractorStrategy: A gap in something the role does not require; one already covered by stated evidence; a smaller gap than another present. Both the requirement and the evidence must be stated so the answer is derivable.
notes: The family that connects this skill to Skill DNA and the roadmap.

factStatement: Two pieces of evidence for the same skill can differ greatly in how much they establish.
familyName: Comparing the strength of two pieces of evidence
measurementObjective: Given two pieces of evidence for one skill, say which establishes more and why.
distractorStrategy: The more impressive-sounding but less verifiable item; the larger but less relevant one; a judgement based on effort rather than on what is shown. Both must be genuine evidence.

factStatement: Widely repeated career advice can fail in a particular situation, for a reason that can be named.
familyName: Identifying why advice fails in a stated case
measurementObjective: Given a situation and a piece of common advice, say why it does not apply.
distractorStrategy: A reason that would apply to any advice; a reason that is true and not why it fails here; a rejection of the advice in general. The situation must contain the specific feature that breaks it.
notes: Framed so the answer is derived from the stated situation, never from the author's view of the advice.

factStatement: Between two reasonable options, the stated constraints decide which is right.
familyName: Choosing between two paths under constraints
measurementObjective: Given two paths and explicit constraints, choose the one that satisfies them and say what it costs.
distractorStrategy: The option that is better in general and violates a stated constraint; one that satisfies the constraints and abandons the goal; one that satisfies everything and is not on offer. Constraints must be explicit and must decide.
notes: Without explicit constraints this is a preference question, which is why they are mandatory here.

factStatement: What someone has learned about the work, and about themselves, can be a reason to change the goal rather than to persist.
familyName: Judging when evidence supports changing the goal
measurementObjective: Given a stated goal and what a student has since learned, say whether the evidence supports revising it.
distractorStrategy: A revision on the strength of one bad experience; persistence in the face of evidence that the work is not what was assumed; a revision to something the evidence says nothing about. Include cases where the evidence supports persisting.
notes: The most important idea in the skill for a first-year, and it must cut both ways or it becomes advice to give up.

factStatement: An error message names what failed and where, and those are different pieces of information.
familyName: Reading what a message actually says
measurementObjective: Given an error message, say what it tells you and what it does not.
distractorStrategy: The location read as the cause — the fundamental confusion, since the reported line is where it surfaced; the message assumed to name the fix; the message dismissed as unreadable. Messages shown verbatim in the stem.
notes: Deliberately domain-light: the message is the object of study, not the program.

factStatement: A refusal to start, a stop partway, and a wrong answer are three different failures.
familyName: Classifying how something failed
measurementObjective: Given a description of what happened, classify the failure.
distractorStrategy: A wrong answer classified as a crash; a crash classified as a refusal to start; the absence of a message taken to mean nothing is wrong. The last is the belief this family exists to break.

factStatement: A message, an output, a recorded value and the state at a moment each answer a different question.
familyName: Choosing the evidence that would answer the question
measurementObjective: Given a question about a fault, say which kind of evidence would answer it.
distractorStrategy: Evidence that would confirm what is already known; evidence about a later stage than the question; more of the same evidence. Choosing what to look at is the first real debugging decision.

factStatement: Investigating a fault requires being able to make it happen on demand, which means knowing the input, the state and the steps.
familyName: Identifying what is needed to reproduce a fault
measurementObjective: Given a report, identify what is missing before the fault can be reproduced.
distractorStrategy: Detail that is present; detail that would be useful later but not for reproducing; a fix proposed instead of the missing information. Pairs with TC_FAM07 from the debugging side.

factStatement: A candidate explanation has to account for everything observed, not just the most obvious symptom.
familyName: Choosing the hypothesis the evidence supports
measurementObjective: Given several observations, choose the explanation consistent with all of them.
distractorStrategy: An explanation fitting the main symptom and contradicting a secondary observation — the essential distractor; one fitting everything but requiring something impossible; one that is a restatement of the symptom.
notes: At least one observation must be inconvenient for the obvious hypothesis.

factStatement: The useful next step is the one that rules out the largest part of what remains possible.
familyName: Choosing the step that narrows the search most
measurementObjective: Given what is known, choose the next check that eliminates the most possibilities.
distractorStrategy: A check confirming what is already known; one that would rule out one possibility of many; one that changes the code before anything has been learned. Same discrimination reasoning as PS_FAM15, applied to investigation.
notes: The defining family of the skill: it is method, and no domain diagnosis family measures it.

factStatement: Checking the middle of a sequence of changes or steps halves what remains to be searched.
familyName: Applying a halving search to find a fault
measurementObjective: Given a range of changes and a working and broken point, say which to check next and how many checks are needed.
distractorStrategy: The next one after the last known good, which is a linear scan; the most recent change, which is a guess; the middle of the whole range rather than of what remains. Same idea as DA_FAM07, applied to history rather than data.

factStatement: A recorded value that is correct at one point and wrong at another places the fault between them.
familyName: Locating a fault from recorded values
measurementObjective: Given values recorded at several points, say between which two the fault lies.
distractorStrategy: The point where the wrong value was first SEEN blamed rather than where it was introduced; a region already shown correct; the last point, because that is where the symptom appeared. Show a short table of values in the stem.

factStatement: If several things are changed and the symptom goes away, nothing has been learned about which mattered.
familyName: Reasoning about what a change told you
measurementObjective: Given several simultaneous changes and a result, say what can and cannot be concluded.
distractorStrategy: One of the changes credited with the fix; all of them declared necessary; the conclusion that the fault is understood. The honest answer — that the experiment was uninformative — must be one option and correct.
notes: Teaches the habit by making its absence visible as lost information.

factStatement: Much debugging time is lost to something believed true that was never verified.
familyName: Identifying the unverified assumption
measurementObjective: Given an account of an investigation, identify what was assumed rather than checked.
distractorStrategy: Something that was checked; something assumed and genuinely irrelevant; the conclusion restated. "The file I edited is the file being run" and "the change was saved" are the productive assumptions.
notes: Connects to BR_FAM11: the change is in the file and not on the screen.

factStatement: A fault that appears sometimes depends on a condition that is varying without being observed.
familyName: Reasoning about a fault that appears sometimes
measurementObjective: Given a fault that occurs on some runs, identify what could be varying.
distractorStrategy: Randomness accepted as the explanation — the answer that stops the investigation; a cause that would fail every time; a cause the account rules out. Something must genuinely vary between runs.

factStatement: If the same thing behaves differently in two places, something about those places differs.
familyName: Finding what differs between two environments
measurementObjective: Given something that works in one place and not another, identify what to compare first.
distractorStrategy: The code blamed although it is identical in both; a difference that exists and cannot cause this symptom; a conclusion that one machine is faulty. Reasoning from the symptom to the class of difference is the measurement.
notes: Draws on CN_FAM05 and BR_FAM06 without requiring either.

factStatement: A fix is demonstrated by understanding why the change works and by the fault no longer reproducing on the case that triggered it.
familyName: Deciding whether a fix has been demonstrated
measurementObjective: Given a change and the observation after it, say whether the fault is fixed.
distractorStrategy: The symptom not appearing on a case that never triggered it; the symptom hidden rather than removed; a change that works for a reason nobody can state. D5 uses a change that genuinely fixes the case tested and not the fault.
notes: The most valuable family in the skill: "it works now" is the commonest false conclusion in programming.

factStatement: A change can remove a symptom while leaving the fault, which then reappears elsewhere.
familyName: Distinguishing a fix from a suppression
measurementObjective: Given two candidate changes, say which addresses the cause and what the other would leave behind.
distractorStrategy: A change that catches and hides the failure; one that special-cases the input that triggered it; one that corrects the cause. All must make the symptom disappear, which is what makes the judgement real.
notes: Every option working is the whole design of this family.

factStatement: Whether to read the code, add recording, bisect the history, or reduce the input depends on what is already known.
familyName: Choosing a debugging approach for the situation
measurementObjective: Given what is known and unknown about a fault, choose the approach that makes progress.
distractorStrategy: Reading the whole codebase where the fault is already localised; bisecting where nothing recently changed; adding recording where the message already says what is needed. Every approach must be a real technique, wrong only for this situation.
notes: The closing family, and the one that requires everything above it.

factStatement: A base fixes which digits may appear: base 2 allows 0 and 1, base 8 allows 0 to 7, base 16 allows 0 to 9 and A to F.
familyName: Recognising which digits a base allows
measurementObjective: Given a written number, say which base it could not possibly be in.
distractorStrategy: A number containing an 8 offered as octal and a 2 offered as binary — the two commonest slips; a hex number rejected because it contains letters, for the student who thinks letters are never digits.
notes: The widest entry point in the skill. A student with no background should still be able to attempt it from the digit rule alone.

factStatement: Each position carries a weight that is a power of the base, counting from zero at the right.
familyName: Naming the weight of a position
measurementObjective: Given a binary number and a marked position, state what that position is worth.
distractorStrategy: Weights counted from the left; counting started at one rather than zero, which shifts every answer by a factor of two; the digit itself offered as its value.

factStatement: A bit holds one of two values and a byte is eight bits; n bits distinguish 2^n different values.
familyName: Recognising what a bit and a byte are
measurementObjective: Given a stated width in bits, say how many distinct values it can hold.
distractorStrategy: 2n offered instead of 2^n — the dominant error; 2^n minus one, which is the largest value rather than the count of values; n^2 for the student pattern-matching on exponents.
notes: Keep widths at or below eight so the answer is recalled or reasoned, never computed on paper.

factStatement: A binary number converts to decimal by adding the weights of the positions holding a 1.
familyName: Converting binary to decimal
measurementObjective: Given a binary number of at most six bits, give its decimal value.
distractorStrategy: The weights read in reverse — the error that only shows on numbers that are not palindromes, so no stem should be one; the count of 1 bits offered as the value; a result one too high from starting the weights at 2.
notes: Every stem must be asymmetric, or reversing the digits produces the same answer and the commonest error goes unmeasured.

factStatement: A decimal number converts to binary by repeatedly taking the largest weight that fits, or equivalently by repeated division by two.
familyName: Converting decimal to binary
measurementObjective: Given a decimal number below 64, give its binary form.
distractorStrategy: Remainders read in the order produced rather than reversed — the classic division-method slip; a bit dropped from the middle; the value of a neighbouring number.

factStatement: One hexadecimal digit stands for exactly four bits, which is why hex is used to write binary compactly.
familyName: Converting between hex and binary by grouping
measurementObjective: Given a hex value or a binary string, produce the other by grouping in fours.
distractorStrategy: Grouping from the left, which misaligns whenever the length is not a multiple of four; groups of three, borrowed from octal; a correct grouping with one digit converted as decimal.
notes: At least one stem should have a bit length that is not a multiple of four, since that is where left-grouping fails.

factStatement: One octal digit stands for exactly three bits, by the same argument that gives hex four.
familyName: Converting between octal and binary
measurementObjective: Given an octal value or a binary string, produce the other by grouping in threes.
distractorStrategy: Groups of four, carried over from hex — the productive confusion between the two grouping rules; grouping from the left; an octal digit above 7 offered as plausible.

factStatement: Binary addition carries when a column reaches two, exactly as decimal carries at ten.
familyName: Adding two binary numbers
measurementObjective: Given two binary numbers of at most five bits, give their sum.
distractorStrategy: A column left as 2 rather than carried; the carry dropped at the leftmost column, which shortens the answer; a bitwise OR result, which agrees with the sum everywhere except where a carry happens.
notes: The OR distractor is the strongest one available here and every stem must involve at least one carry, or it does not discriminate.

conceptName: What a fixed width can hold
factStatement: An unsigned field of n bits represents the values 0 to 2^n minus 1, and nothing outside them.
familyName: Deriving the range a width allows
measurementObjective: Given a width in bits, give the largest value it can hold, or the width a stated value needs.
distractorStrategy: 2^n offered as the maximum — the off-by-one that this family exists to catch; a width one too small for a value that sits exactly on a power of two; the count of values given where the maximum was asked.
notes: Values on a power-of-two boundary are the discriminating stems; 256 needing nine bits rather than eight is the canonical case.

factStatement: Shifting a binary number one place left doubles it and one place right halves it, discarding what falls off the end.
familyName: Predicting the effect of a shift
measurementObjective: Given a value and a shift, state the resulting value.
distractorStrategy: The direction reversed, so the value halves where it should double; the discarded bit assumed to wrap around to the other end; a right shift of an odd number rounded up rather than truncated.
notes: Odd numbers shifted right are the stem that separates understanding from the memorised "shift means multiply".

factStatement: A wrong conversion is usually right until one identifiable step, and the step can be found by checking each in turn.
familyName: Locating the step a conversion went wrong at
measurementObjective: Given a worked conversion with a wrong result, identify the step that introduced the error.
distractorStrategy: A step that is correct but unusual, which attracts students who look for the odd-looking line; the step after the real error, where the wrong value first becomes visible; the final step, which is merely where the wrong answer is written down.
notes: The distinction between where an error was made and where it became visible is the measurement; every stem must separate the two by at least one step.

factStatement: The same digits denote different values in different bases, so a number written without its base is ambiguous.
familyName: Diagnosing a value misread in the wrong base
measurementObjective: Given a situation where a value came out wrong, decide whether a base was assumed rather than stated.
distractorStrategy: An arithmetic slip offered where the fault is interpretive; the claim that the value is simply invalid; a base confusion named in the wrong direction, which produces a different wrong value than the one observed.
notes: Strongest stems use digit strings that are legal in several bases — 11, 101, 20 — so the ambiguity is real rather than asserted.

conceptName: What a fixed width can hold
factStatement: A value that exceeds its width does not become large; the bits that do not fit are lost and the value wraps.
familyName: Reasoning about a value that exceeds its width
measurementObjective: Given a fixed width and an operation that exceeds it, say what is stored and why.
distractorStrategy: The true mathematical sum, which is the answer a student gives who has not accepted that the width is a hard limit; the maximum value, as though the field saturated; an error being raised, which is a language decision rather than a property of the representation.
notes: Saturation is a real behaviour in some hardware, so it is a fair distractor rather than an absurd one — say plainly in the stem that the extra bits are discarded.

factStatement: Choosing a width trades range against space, and choosing a base trades compactness against readability; neither has one right answer without a stated requirement.
familyName: Choosing a width or base for a stated requirement
measurementObjective: Given a requirement with stated limits, choose the representation that meets it without waste.
distractorStrategy: A width that fits today's largest value exactly, leaving no room for the growth the stem states; a far larger width justified by safety where the stem constrains space; a base chosen for familiarity against a stated compactness requirement.
notes: Every option must be defensible under some requirement, so the stem must state the requirement precisely enough to settle it.

factStatement: The same positional reasoning explains anything packed into bits — flags, permissions, colour channels — not only numbers.
familyName: Applying binary reasoning to an unfamiliar encoding
measurementObjective: Given a described bit encoding the student has not seen, work out what a given pattern means or which pattern is needed.
distractorStrategy: The pattern read as a plain decimal number rather than as independent flags; two flags combined by addition where they overlap; the bit order reversed relative to the stem's own statement of it.
notes: The encoding must be fully defined in the stem — this measures transfer of positional reasoning, not recall of any real permission scheme.

factStatement: A set is determined by which things are in it; order and repetition do not change it.
familyName: Recognising when two sets are the same set
measurementObjective: Given two written collections, say whether they denote the same set.
distractorStrategy: Two listings differing only in order treated as different — the commonest first answer; a repeated element treated as adding a member; a set and a list of the same items treated as interchangeable.
notes: The anchor family. Keep every set to at most four elements written out in full.

factStatement: Union answers "in either", intersection "in both", and difference "in this one and not the other".
familyName: Naming the operation a description calls for
measurementObjective: Given a description in words, name the set operation it describes.
distractorStrategy: Union and intersection exchanged, which the words "and" and "or" actively encourage — "students taking maths and physics" is an intersection; difference offered where the description is symmetric.
notes: Everyday "and" meaning intersection is the productive trap and at least two stems should use it.

factStatement: An element belongs to a set; a subset is contained in it, and the empty set is a subset of every set.
familyName: Distinguishing membership from containment
measurementObjective: Given a set and a candidate, say whether it is an element, a subset, both, or neither.
distractorStrategy: An element offered as a subset and a one-element set offered as a member — the two halves of the same confusion; the empty set denied as a subset.
notes: Sets that contain sets are the discriminating stem, but keep to one level of nesting.

factStatement: Applying an operation to two listed sets produces a determinate third set.
familyName: Computing a union or intersection
measurementObjective: Given two small sets, give the result of a named operation.
distractorStrategy: The other operation's result; a union with the shared elements listed twice; a result that silently drops an element present in only one set.

factStatement: Difference is not symmetric: what is in A and not B is generally not what is in B and not A.
familyName: Applying difference in the stated direction
measurementObjective: Given two sets, give the difference asked for rather than its reverse.
distractorStrategy: The reversed difference, which is the whole point of the family; the symmetric difference, which is a real operation and a fair confusion; the intersection removed from the union.
notes: The two differences must be unequal in every stem, or the family measures nothing.

factStatement: A complement is only defined against a stated universe; change the universe and the complement changes.
familyName: Taking a complement against a stated universe
measurementObjective: Given a universe and a set, give the complement, or say why it cannot be given.
distractorStrategy: A complement taken against an assumed universe rather than the stated one; everything not mentioned anywhere in the question; the set itself, for the student who reverses the operation.
notes: One stem should give two different universes for the same set, which makes the dependence impossible to miss.

factStatement: Each region of a two- or three-circle diagram corresponds to one expression built from the sets.
familyName: Matching a described region to its expression
measurementObjective: Given a described region in words, choose the expression that denotes exactly it.
distractorStrategy: An expression covering the region plus one neighbouring region — the error of describing "only A" as "A"; the complement of the intended region; the right regions joined by the wrong operation.
notes: Regions are described in words, never drawn: this bank carries no images, and "in A but in neither of the others" is unambiguous without one.

factStatement: The size of a union is the sum of the sizes minus the size of the overlap, because the overlap is otherwise counted twice.
familyName: Counting the members of a union
measurementObjective: Given the sizes of two sets and their overlap, give the size of their union.
distractorStrategy: The plain sum, which double counts — the error the rule exists to prevent; the overlap subtracted twice; the sum of the two exclusive parts, omitting the overlap altogether.
notes: Keep the numbers small enough that a wrong answer is a wrong method rather than a wrong sum.

factStatement: Knowing two sets are not disjoint does not say how large the overlap is, and many questions are unanswerable without it.
familyName: Deciding whether the overlap is settled
measurementObjective: Given partial information about two sets, decide what can and cannot be concluded about their union.
distractorStrategy: A single number where a range is the honest answer; disjointness assumed because nothing said otherwise; total overlap assumed from the smaller set fitting inside the larger.
notes: "It cannot be determined" must be the correct answer in some stems and a distractor in others, or the family teaches a reflex.

conceptName: Sets in the tools students use
factStatement: Combining filters or query conditions performs union, intersection and difference on the rows they select.
familyName: Reading a combined filter as a set operation
measurementObjective: Given filters combined in a stated way, say which rows are selected.
distractorStrategy: AND and OR exchanged, which selects far too many or too few rows; a negation applied to one condition rather than the whole; the rows matching either condition offered where both were required.
notes: Filters are described in plain words rather than SQL, so this measures the set reasoning and not SQL_BASICS.

factStatement: A total that exceeds the number of things available is the signature of counting an overlap twice.
familyName: Diagnosing a count that came out too high
measurementObjective: Given a stated count that is impossible, identify why it is wrong.
distractorStrategy: An arithmetic slip proposed where the method is at fault; the data declared wrong, which is the answer that requires no reasoning; the overlap named but in the wrong direction.

factStatement: Choosing the wrong operation yields a perfectly well-formed set, which is why the error survives review.
familyName: Diagnosing a requirement met by the wrong operation
measurementObjective: Given a requirement and an implementation that does not meet it, say which operation should have been used.
distractorStrategy: The operation actually used, restated as though correct; an operation that happens to agree on the example given but not in general; a correct operation applied to the wrong pair of sets.
notes: The strongest stems are ones where the wrong operation gives the right answer on the sample data and the wrong one in general.

factStatement: A claim about all sets is refuted by a single example, and no number of confirming examples establishes it.
familyName: Testing whether an identity holds for all sets
measurementObjective: Given a proposed set identity, decide whether it always holds and identify the example that settles it.
distractorStrategy: A confirming example offered as proof; a counterexample that does not actually violate the claim; the claim accepted because it holds whenever the sets are disjoint, which is exactly the case that hides most failures.
notes: This family replaces the De Morgan family the design originally had here, because two other skills in this batch measure De Morgan and would have duplicated it.

factStatement: A requirement stated in words corresponds to one set expression, and near misses select the wrong things.
familyName: Building the expression a requirement needs
measurementObjective: Given a requirement in words, choose the set expression that captures it exactly.
distractorStrategy: An expression that is correct except at the boundary the requirement turns on — those who qualify for both, or for neither; an expression matching a looser reading of the same sentence; the complement of the intended one.
notes: The requirement must be worded so that exactly one expression fits; ambiguity here makes the item unanswerable rather than hard.

conceptName: Sets in the tools students use
factStatement: A situation with overlapping groups can be modelled as sets whether or not it is presented that way.
familyName: Modelling an unfamiliar situation as sets
measurementObjective: Given a described situation with no set vocabulary in it, choose the modelling that answers the question asked.
distractorStrategy: A model that treats overlapping groups as disjoint; one that models the wrong universe; one that is correct but cannot answer the specific question the stem asks.
notes: No stem may use the words union, intersection or set — the transfer is the measurement.

factStatement: In an ordered pair the first and second positions mean different things, so swapping them gives a different pair.
familyName: Recognising that a pair has a direction
measurementObjective: Given a described correspondence, say which ordered pair records it.
distractorStrategy: The reversed pair, which is the only distractor that matters here; the pair written as a set, discarding the order; both elements taken from the same side of the correspondence.
notes: The correspondence in the stem must be asymmetric — "is the capital of" rather than "is next to".

conceptName: What goes in and what comes out
factStatement: The domain is the set of values that go in and the range is the set of values that actually come out.
familyName: Naming the domain and range of a mapping
measurementObjective: Given a mapping listed as pairs, state its domain or its range.
distractorStrategy: Domain and range exchanged; a repeated output listed twice, since the range is a set; the pairs themselves offered where a set of values was asked.

conceptName: When a relation is a function
factStatement: A relation is a function when every input has exactly one output; an input with two outputs disqualifies it, an output shared by two inputs does not.
familyName: Deciding whether a relation is a function
measurementObjective: Given a set of pairs, say whether it defines a function.
distractorStrategy: A mapping rejected because two inputs share an output — the mirror-image error that this family exists to separate from the real rule; one accepted despite a repeated input with different outputs.
notes: Every stem must contain a shared output somewhere, so that the wrong rule is always available to be applied.

factStatement: Evaluating a function at a value substitutes that value wherever the input appears.
familyName: Evaluating a function at a value
measurementObjective: Given a rule and an input, give the output.
distractorStrategy: The rule applied to the output rather than the input; an operation order slip inside the rule; the input returned unchanged.
notes: Rules stay to one or two operations — this measures substitution, not arithmetic.

factStatement: A function may be given as a table or a list of pairs rather than a formula, and is used the same way.
familyName: Reading a function given as a table
measurementObjective: Given a mapping written as a table, give the output for a stated input.
distractorStrategy: The table read backwards, giving the input for a stated output; an adjacent row, for the student tracking by position; a value not in the table at all, offered for an input outside the domain.
notes: One stem should ask for an input outside the domain, where "undefined" is the honest answer.

conceptName: How a mapping distributes its outputs
factStatement: A function is one-to-one when no two different inputs give the same output.
familyName: Deciding whether a mapping is one-to-one
measurementObjective: Given a mapping, say whether it is one-to-one and name the pair that decides it.
distractorStrategy: The function test applied instead — rejecting for a repeated input rather than a repeated output; a mapping called one-to-one because each input has one output, which is true of every function.

conceptName: How a mapping distributes its outputs
factStatement: The values a function actually produces may be fewer than the values it is allowed to produce.
familyName: Distinguishing what is produced from what is permitted
measurementObjective: Given a function and a stated target set, say which values are never produced.
distractorStrategy: The target set offered as the range; the domain offered as the range; a value that is produced, listed among those that are not.
notes: Squaring over a small integer domain is the clearest stem: negatives are permitted and never produced.

factStatement: Applying f then g generally gives a different result from applying g then f.
familyName: Composing two functions in the stated order
measurementObjective: Given two rules and an input, give the result of applying them in the order stated.
distractorStrategy: The other order, which is the measurement; the two rules applied to the input separately and combined; only the outer rule applied.
notes: The two orders must give different results in every stem, so no pair of rules that commute.

factStatement: A mapping can be reversed only if no output is shared, because a shared output has no single input to return to.
familyName: Deciding whether a mapping can be reversed
measurementObjective: Given a mapping, say whether it has an inverse and why.
distractorStrategy: An inverse claimed for a mapping with a shared output, with the ambiguity unnoticed; reversal refused because the rule is hard to undo algebraically, which is a different question; the inverse of the wrong direction.

factStatement: A dictionary, an index and a database key are functions: one value in, at most one value out.
familyName: Reading a lookup structure as a mapping
measurementObjective: Given a described lookup, say what its domain, range or function property is.
distractorStrategy: Keys and values exchanged; a structure allowing duplicate keys assumed to be a function; the claim that a lookup with two keys mapping to one value is not a function.
notes: Described in plain words rather than any language's syntax, so this does not become a Python question.

factStatement: A single input appearing twice with different outputs is enough to disqualify a mapping, however large it is.
familyName: Finding the pair that stops a relation being a function
measurementObjective: Given a relation that is not a function, identify the specific pair responsible.
distractorStrategy: A pair sharing an output with another, which breaks nothing; the second occurrence named where the stem asks which pair conflicts with which; a pair that is merely unusual.

factStatement: Composing in the wrong order produces a value rather than an error, so the fault shows only in the result.
familyName: Diagnosing a composition applied in the wrong order
measurementObjective: Given an expected and an actual result, decide whether the order of application explains the difference.
distractorStrategy: An arithmetic error proposed where the order is at fault; the input blamed; the right diagnosis attached to the wrong one of the two rules.
notes: The actual result must be exactly what the reversed order gives, so the diagnosis is verifiable from the stem.

factStatement: Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity are claims about every member or every pair, so one failure decides them.
familyName: Testing a small relation for a stated property
measurementObjective: Given a relation on a small set, say whether a named property holds and what settles it.
distractorStrategy: A property accepted because it holds for most pairs; symmetry and transitivity confused; reflexivity judged from one element rather than all.
notes: Relations are given on sets of three or four elements so exhaustive checking is feasible in the head.

factStatement: Whether a mapping must be one-to-one is decided by what the data is for, not by the mathematics.
familyName: Choosing a mapping that meets a stated requirement
measurementObjective: Given a requirement, choose the mapping whose properties satisfy it.
distractorStrategy: A mapping that is one-to-one where the requirement does not need it and pays for it; one that is not, where reversal is required; one whose domain excludes cases the requirement states will occur.
notes: Every option must be a legitimate mapping; only the requirement separates them.

factStatement: Many situations are mappings without being described as such, and the questions asked of them are function questions.
familyName: Recognising mapping structure in an unfamiliar situation
measurementObjective: Given a situation using no mapping vocabulary, answer a question that depends on its function properties.
distractorStrategy: An answer that would hold if the mapping were one-to-one when the stem says it is not; the direction of the mapping reversed; a conclusion about the domain drawn from facts about the range.
notes: No stem may use the words function, domain or range — recognising the structure is the measurement.

conceptName: Statements that have a truth value
factStatement: A proposition is a statement that is either true or false; questions, commands and opinions are not propositions.
familyName: Recognising what can carry a truth value
measurementObjective: Given several sentences, say which one is a proposition.
distractorStrategy: A question and a command, which have no truth value; a statement whose truth is unknown, which IS a proposition and is the productive near miss.
notes: "Unknown truth value" versus "no truth value" is the distinction worth measuring here.

factStatement: AND is true only when both parts are true, OR when at least one is, and NOT reverses the value.
familyName: Naming the connective a description requires
measurementObjective: Given a condition described in words, name the connective that expresses it.
distractorStrategy: OR offered as exclusive, which everyday speech encourages — "tea or coffee" excludes both, logic's OR does not; AND and OR exchanged.
notes: Inclusive OR is the fact most often unlearned and at least two stems should turn on it.

factStatement: A truth table has one row for every combination of values, so n variables give 2^n rows.
familyName: Reading the shape of a truth table
measurementObjective: Given a number of variables, or a row of a table, state the row count or the value recorded.
distractorStrategy: 2n rows rather than 2^n; n^2 rows; a row count that omits the all-false row, which students often forget to write.

factStatement: A compound statement has a determinate value once the values of its parts are fixed.
familyName: Evaluating a compound under stated values
measurementObjective: Given values for the variables, give the value of a compound expression.
distractorStrategy: AND evaluated as OR; the value of one part offered as the value of the whole; "cannot be determined" where every variable has been given a value.
notes: Expressions stay to two connectives; longer ones measure care rather than understanding.

factStatement: A negation applies to exactly the expression it encloses, and moving that boundary changes the meaning.
familyName: Applying a negation to the right scope
measurementObjective: Given a negated compound, give its value or say what it denies.
distractorStrategy: The negation applied to the first part only — the dominant scope error; both parts negated with the connective left unchanged, which is the classic half-done De Morgan.

factStatement: An if-then statement is false only when the first part is true and the second false; a false first part makes it true.
familyName: Judging when an if-then statement is false
measurementObjective: Given values for both parts, say whether the implication holds.
distractorStrategy: An implication with a false first part judged false — the single most common error in the topic; the implication treated as symmetric; "undetermined" offered for the vacuous case.
notes: The vacuously true case must appear in at least three of this family's questions; it is the whole difficulty.

factStatement: Filling a table means evaluating the expression once for each combination, and the completed column is the expression's meaning.
familyName: Completing a row or column of a truth table
measurementObjective: Given a partially filled table, supply the missing entry or identify the completed column.
distractorStrategy: A column belonging to a related expression — the AND column offered for an OR; a column correct except in the row where the two differ; a column read from the wrong row order.
notes: Rows are written out in the stem in a stated order, since this bank cannot rely on a conventional layout.

conceptName: When two expressions say the same thing
factStatement: Two expressions are equivalent when they agree on every combination, not merely on the cases someone happened to check.
familyName: Deciding whether two expressions are equivalent
measurementObjective: Given two expressions, say whether they always agree and name the row that settles it.
distractorStrategy: Two expressions agreeing on three rows of four declared equivalent; the disagreeing row named wrongly; equivalence denied because the expressions look different.
notes: Pairs that agree everywhere except one row are the discriminating stems.

factStatement: Reversing an if-then statement or negating both its parts changes what it says; doing both together does not.
familyName: Choosing the form that preserves meaning
measurementObjective: Given an if-then statement, choose the restatement that says the same thing.
distractorStrategy: The converse, which is the reflex answer; the inverse; the original with only one part negated. All four options must be about the same two statements.

factStatement: Which branch of a decision runs is settled entirely by the truth value of its condition.
familyName: Predicting which branch a condition selects
measurementObjective: Given a condition described in words and stated values, say which branch runs.
distractorStrategy: The branch that would run under the opposite connective; both branches claimed to run; the branch chosen by everyday reading of "or" as exclusive.
notes: Conditions are stated in words, not code — CONDITIONALS_BASICS measures the code, this measures the logic under it.

conceptName: When two expressions say the same thing
factStatement: Some expressions are true on every row and others false on every row, whatever their variables are.
familyName: Identifying an expression that cannot vary
measurementObjective: Given an expression, say whether it is always true, always false, or depends on its variables.
distractorStrategy: An expression true on three rows of four called always true; always-false and always-true exchanged; an expression that does vary, called constant because it usually comes out true.

factStatement: A condition using the wrong connective is valid and runs; it simply selects the wrong cases.
familyName: Diagnosing a condition that selects the wrong cases
measurementObjective: Given a requirement and the cases a condition actually selects, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: A fault named in the values rather than the connective; the right fault attributed to the wrong part of the condition; a fix that repairs the reported case and breaks another.
notes: The stem must state the cases wrongly selected, so the diagnosis is checkable rather than guessable.

factStatement: Denying "both" gives "at least one is not", and denying "either" gives "neither" — the connective changes as well as the parts.
familyName: Working out which cases a denied condition admits
measurementObjective: Given a compound condition and its denial, say which cases now satisfy it.
distractorStrategy: Both parts negated with the connective unchanged — the half-done rule, and by far the most attractive wrong answer; only the first part negated; the original condition restated.
notes: This is one of the two De Morgan families in the batch. It works in truth values and admitted cases; the BOOLEAN_ALGEBRA one works in algebraic form. Neither may be answerable by the other's method.

conceptName: Writing the condition a rule requires
factStatement: A stated rule admits exactly one condition; conditions that are nearly right differ at the boundary cases.
familyName: Choosing the condition that expresses a rule exactly
measurementObjective: Given a rule in words, choose the condition that admits exactly the intended cases.
distractorStrategy: A condition correct except for the case satisfying both criteria; one correct except for the case satisfying neither; one that reads naturally in English and admits more cases than the rule allows.
notes: The rule must be stated so the boundary cases are decidable, or the item has no defensible key.

conceptName: Writing the condition a rule requires
factStatement: Anything that combines yes-or-no facts — permissions, filters, eligibility rules — obeys the same rules as a compound statement.
familyName: Applying truth-functional reasoning in an unfamiliar setting
measurementObjective: Given a rule system the student has not seen, work out what it grants or refuses in a stated case.
distractorStrategy: An outcome that follows only if a stated rule is read as exclusive; one that requires a rule the stem does not give; one derived from the rules applied in the wrong order where the stem fixes an order.
notes: The rule system must be fully specified in the stem; this measures transfer, not knowledge of any real system.

factStatement: A Boolean variable takes only 0 or 1, and every expression built from them takes only 0 or 1.
familyName: Recognising what a Boolean variable can be
measurementObjective: Given a described quantity, say whether it can be represented by a Boolean variable.
distractorStrategy: A quantity with three states offered as Boolean; a count offered as Boolean because it is a number; a genuinely two-state quantity rejected because it is not written as 0 and 1.

factStatement: In Boolean notation the plus sign means OR, the product means AND, and a bar means NOT — despite the arithmetic they resemble.
familyName: Reading Boolean notation as operations
measurementObjective: Given a Boolean expression, say which operations it applies.
distractorStrategy: Plus read as arithmetic addition, so 1 + 1 is given as 2 — the defining confusion of the topic; product read as OR; the bar read as applying to the whole expression when it covers one variable.
notes: 1 + 1 = 1 is the single most useful stem in this family and must appear.

factStatement: Each gate implements one operation: AND outputs 1 only when all inputs are 1, OR when any is, NOT reverses, XOR outputs 1 when the inputs differ.
familyName: Recognising what a named gate does
measurementObjective: Given a gate and its inputs, give its output.
distractorStrategy: XOR answered as OR, which agree except when both inputs are 1 — so that case must be used; NAND answered as AND; a gate's output inverted.
notes: Gates are named in words. Nothing in this bank may depend on a drawn symbol.

factStatement: In Boolean expressions the product is applied before the sum unless brackets say otherwise, as in ordinary algebra.
familyName: Evaluating a Boolean expression for given inputs
measurementObjective: Given values for the variables, give the value of the expression.
distractorStrategy: The expression evaluated strictly left to right, ignoring precedence; a bar applied after the operation it should precede; an arithmetic result such as 2.
notes: Every stem must have a different value under left-to-right evaluation, or precedence goes unmeasured.

factStatement: A OR 1 is 1 and A AND 0 is 0 whatever A is, while A OR 0 and A AND 1 leave A unchanged.
familyName: Applying the laws involving 0 and 1
measurementObjective: Given an expression containing a constant, give the simplified form.
distractorStrategy: The two pairs exchanged, so A OR 1 is given as A — the commonest slip; the constant simply deleted; the variable dropped where the constant dominates.

factStatement: A OR A and A AND A both give A, while A OR its complement gives 1 and A AND its complement gives 0.
familyName: Applying the idempotent and complement laws
measurementObjective: Given an expression combining a variable with itself or its complement, give the result.
distractorStrategy: A OR A given as 2A or as 1, importing arithmetic; the complement laws exchanged, so A AND its complement is given as 1; the complement itself offered as the answer.

conceptName: Changing the form without changing the value
factStatement: In Boolean algebra the sum distributes over the product as well as the product over the sum, which ordinary arithmetic does not allow.
familyName: Expanding or factoring a Boolean expression
measurementObjective: Given an expression, choose the correctly distributed or factored equivalent.
distractorStrategy: A distribution valid in arithmetic but applied to the wrong operation here; a term dropped during expansion; a factoring that changes which variable is common.
notes: The sum distributing over the product has no arithmetic analogue and is the discriminating case.

conceptName: Changing the form without changing the value
factStatement: A OR (A AND B) is just A, because whenever the second part is true the first already is.
familyName: Recognising a term that adds nothing
measurementObjective: Given an expression where one term is redundant, give the reduced form.
distractorStrategy: The wrong term absorbed, leaving the product; absorption applied where the variable appears complemented and the law does not hold; the expression expanded rather than reduced.
notes: One stem should look like absorption but involve a complement, where the reduction is invalid.

factStatement: Each step of a simplification is licensed by one law, and a step licensed by none is not a simplification.
familyName: Naming the law that licenses a step
measurementObjective: Given one step of a simplification, name the law that justifies it.
distractorStrategy: A law that is real and does not apply to this step; a law that would license the reverse step; a law named correctly for a different line of the same working.

factStatement: A described arrangement of gates corresponds to one Boolean expression, and the expression to one arrangement.
familyName: Translating between a described circuit and an expression
measurementObjective: Given gates described in words, give the expression they compute.
distractorStrategy: The gates composed in the reverse order; an expression matching the same gates wired in parallel rather than in series; the inversion attached to the wrong input.
notes: Circuits are described as prose — "the output of the first gate feeds one input of the second" — never drawn.

factStatement: A simplification that imports an arithmetic rule or mis-scopes a bar produces an expression that still looks well formed.
familyName: Finding the step that is not licensed
measurementObjective: Given a worked simplification whose result is wrong, identify the invalid step.
distractorStrategy: A valid but unusual step; the step where the error becomes visible rather than where it was made; the last step, which merely records the wrong result.

factStatement: Two Boolean expressions are equal exactly when they agree on every combination of inputs, which for two or three variables can simply be checked.
familyName: Verifying that a rewrite preserved the value
measurementObjective: Given an original and a rewritten expression, say whether they are equal and where they differ if not.
distractorStrategy: A rewrite agreeing on three of four input combinations declared equal; the differing combination named wrongly; equality denied because the forms look different.
notes: This family and PL_FAM08 both check agreement across cases, so every stem here must be algebraic rewriting rather than two independently written expressions.

conceptName: Pushing a bar through an expression
factStatement: The complement of a product is the sum of the complements, and the complement of a sum is the product of the complements.
familyName: Rewriting a complemented group
measurementObjective: Given a complemented product or sum, give the equivalent form with the bar pushed inward.
distractorStrategy: Each variable complemented with the operation left unchanged — the half-applied rule; the operation swapped with the variables left alone; a double complement left in place rather than cancelled.
notes: The batch's second De Morgan family, working purely in algebraic form. PL_FAM13 works in admitted cases; neither may be answerable by the other's method.

factStatement: Among equivalent expressions, which counts as simplest depends on what is being minimised — terms, variables, or gates of a given kind.
familyName: Choosing the best form for a stated criterion
measurementObjective: Given equivalent expressions and a stated criterion, choose the one that best meets it.
distractorStrategy: A shorter expression that is not equivalent — correctness must be checked before simplicity; the simplest by a criterion other than the one stated; the original, offered as already minimal.
notes: At least one distractor must be non-equivalent, so that a student who optimises before verifying is caught.

factStatement: The same laws reduce any expression over two-valued quantities, including the conditions in a program and the rules in a permission system.
familyName: Simplifying a two-valued expression in an unfamiliar setting
measurementObjective: Given a redundant rule set the student has not seen, choose the reduced form that admits the same cases.
distractorStrategy: A reduction that drops a case the original admitted; one that admits an extra case; one that is equivalent but no simpler, offered where the stem asks for a reduction.
notes: No stem may use Boolean notation — the transfer is recognising that the laws apply at all.

factStatement: A matrix is described by its rows then its columns, in that order.
familyName: Stating the dimensions of a matrix
measurementObjective: Given a matrix written out, give its dimensions.
distractorStrategy: Columns given before rows — the only error most students make here; the total count of entries offered as a dimension; the larger dimension given first regardless of which it is.
notes: Non-square matrices only; a square one cannot distinguish the right answer from the reversed one.

factStatement: An entry is located by its row first and its column second, and the two indices are not interchangeable.
familyName: Locating an entry by its indices
measurementObjective: Given a matrix and a pair of indices, give the entry.
distractorStrategy: The entry at the transposed position; an entry one row or column away, from counting from zero where the stem counts from one; the entry with the same value elsewhere.
notes: The stem must state whether indices start at one or zero, since the students meet both conventions.

factStatement: A square matrix has equal dimensions, a zero matrix has every entry zero, and an identity matrix has ones on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere.
familyName: Recognising a named kind of matrix
measurementObjective: Given a matrix, say which named kind it is.
distractorStrategy: A matrix of all ones offered as the identity — the commonest confusion; a diagonal matrix with entries other than one called an identity; a non-square matrix called square because it looks regular.

factStatement: Two matrices can be added only if they have the same dimensions, and then entries in the same position are added.
familyName: Adding two matrices, or saying why it is impossible
measurementObjective: Given two matrices, give their sum or state that it is undefined.
distractorStrategy: A sum produced for mismatched shapes by padding or truncating; entries added along the wrong pairing; the difference offered as the sum.
notes: One stem in this family must have mismatched shapes, so "undefined" is sometimes the key.

factStatement: Multiplying a matrix by a number multiplies every entry by it, leaving the shape unchanged.
familyName: Multiplying a matrix by a number
measurementObjective: Given a matrix and a scalar, give the product.
distractorStrategy: Only the first row or the diagonal multiplied; the scalar added to every entry instead; the shape changed.

conceptName: Turning a matrix on its side
factStatement: The transpose turns each row into a column, so an m by n matrix becomes n by m.
familyName: Transposing a matrix
measurementObjective: Given a matrix, give its transpose or the transpose's dimensions.
distractorStrategy: The matrix with its rows reversed rather than transposed; the dimensions left unchanged; the transpose of only part of the matrix.

factStatement: An m by n matrix can multiply an n by p matrix, giving an m by p result; if the inner dimensions differ the product does not exist.
familyName: Deciding whether a product exists and what shape it has
measurementObjective: Given two shapes, say whether the product is defined and give its dimensions.
distractorStrategy: The outer dimensions checked instead of the inner; the result given as the inner dimensions; a product declared defined because it is defined the other way round.
notes: Pairs where one order is defined and the other is not are the discriminating stems.

factStatement: The entry in row i and column j of a product is formed from row i of the first matrix and column j of the second.
familyName: Computing one entry of a product
measurementObjective: Given two small matrices and a position, give that entry of their product.
distractorStrategy: The entrywise product of the two matrices at that position — the intuitive but wrong operation; row paired with row rather than row with column; the entry from the product taken in the other order.
notes: Two by two matrices with single-digit entries throughout; the measurement is the pairing rule, not the arithmetic.

factStatement: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: AB and BA are generally different, and may not both exist.
familyName: Reasoning about the order of a product
measurementObjective: Given two matrices, say whether swapping the order changes or invalidates the product.
distractorStrategy: Commutativity assumed from arithmetic; the claim that order never matters when both products exist; the claim that order matters only when the shapes differ.

factStatement: An image, a board and a spreadsheet region are grids of values addressed by row and column, which is what a matrix is.
familyName: Addressing a value in a grid of data
measurementObjective: Given a described grid, say which position holds a stated value or what a position holds.
distractorStrategy: Coordinates given as across-then-down where the stem specifies row-then-column; an off-by-one from a different index origin; a position outside the grid.
notes: The clash between graphics conventions and matrix conventions is real; the stem must state which one is in force.

factStatement: When an operation is undefined it is because specific dimensions fail to meet its requirement, and the requirement can be named.
familyName: Explaining why an operation cannot be performed
measurementObjective: Given an attempted operation that fails, name the requirement that is not met.
distractorStrategy: The addition requirement given for a multiplication failure and vice versa; the requirement stated for the wrong pair of dimensions; the claim that the entries rather than the shapes are at fault.

factStatement: Reading a grid column-first rather than row-first yields real values from the wrong places, so nothing looks obviously wrong.
familyName: Diagnosing a row and column swap
measurementObjective: Given expected and actual values from a grid, decide whether the indices were exchanged.
distractorStrategy: An off-by-one proposed where a swap is at fault; the data blamed; a swap diagnosed where the observed values are inconsistent with one.
notes: The observed value must be exactly the transposed entry, so the diagnosis is settled by the stem rather than by plausibility.

factStatement: Some facts about a product — its shape, the effect of multiplying by an identity or a zero matrix — follow from structure without computing entries.
familyName: Concluding something about a product without computing it
measurementObjective: Given matrices described by their structure, state what follows about a product.
distractorStrategy: A conclusion that would need the entries; the identity assumed to leave a product unchanged in an order where the shapes forbid it; a zero matrix assumed to make every product square.

conceptName: Whether a matrix is the right tool
factStatement: A matrix suits data that is genuinely rectangular and uniformly typed; ragged or heterogeneous data is misrepresented by one.
familyName: Judging whether a matrix fits the data
measurementObjective: Given described data, decide whether a matrix is an appropriate representation and why.
distractorStrategy: A matrix accepted for ragged data on the grounds that missing entries can be padded, which changes what the data says; rejected for data that is genuinely rectangular; accepted for the wrong reason.
notes: Padding being a real technique is what makes that option a fair distractor rather than an obvious one.

conceptName: Whether a matrix is the right tool
factStatement: Row-and-column reasoning answers questions about any grid, including ones never described as matrices.
familyName: Applying row and column reasoning to an unfamiliar grid
measurementObjective: Given an unfamiliar grid problem, choose the operation or reading that answers it.
distractorStrategy: An operation that answers a similar but different question about the grid; the right operation applied along the wrong axis; a reading that assumes the grid is square when the stem says otherwise.
notes: No stem may use the word matrix, transpose or dimension — recognising the structure is the measurement.

factStatement: The sample space is the complete list of outcomes, and every outcome appears in it exactly once.
familyName: Identifying the outcomes of a described trial
measurementObjective: Given a described trial, say what its sample space is or how many outcomes it has.
distractorStrategy: A list omitting an outcome the student considers unlikely; two outcomes merged because they share a property; the number of things involved offered as the number of outcomes.
notes: Coins, dice and small draws only — the trial must be describable in one sentence.

factStatement: An event is a set of outcomes, so an event may contain one outcome, several, or none.
familyName: Identifying which outcomes an event covers
measurementObjective: Given a described event, say which outcomes it contains.
distractorStrategy: An event limited to one outcome where several qualify; the complement listed; an outcome included that fails the stated description at the boundary — "more than 4" taken to include 4.

factStatement: Every probability lies between 0 and 1, and the probabilities of all outcomes sum to exactly 1.
familyName: Recognising an impossible probability or distribution
measurementObjective: Given a stated probability or a set of them, say whether it could be correct.
distractorStrategy: A set summing to slightly more or less than one, which requires the check rather than a glance; a negative value; a percentage above one hundred offered as valid because it is written as a percentage.

factStatement: When outcomes are equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of outcomes in it divided by the total.
familyName: Computing a probability from equally likely outcomes
measurementObjective: Given a trial with equally likely outcomes, give the probability of a described event.
distractorStrategy: Favourable divided by unfavourable rather than by the total — odds given where a probability was asked; the complement; a boundary outcome miscounted.

factStatement: The probability that an event does not happen is one minus the probability that it does.
familyName: Finding the probability of the opposite event
measurementObjective: Given the probability of an event, give the probability that it does not occur.
distractorStrategy: The original value returned unchanged; the reciprocal; the value subtracted from the total number of outcomes rather than from one.
notes: The complement is most useful when the event is awkward to count directly; at least one stem should be of that kind.

factStatement: The mean is the total divided by how many values there are, so every value influences it.
familyName: Computing and interpreting a mean
measurementObjective: Given a small set of values, give the mean or say how it responds to a change.
distractorStrategy: The middle value offered as the mean; division by one fewer than the count; the total offered without dividing.
notes: Five or six single-digit values, chosen so the mean is exact — a repeating decimal turns this into an arithmetic question.

factStatement: The median is the middle value once sorted, averaging the two middle values when the count is even; the mode is the value occurring most often.
familyName: Finding the median and the mode
measurementObjective: Given a small set of values, give its median or its mode.
distractorStrategy: The middle value taken without sorting first — the dominant error; one of the two middle values given where the count is even; the frequency of the mode given rather than the mode itself.
notes: Values must be presented unsorted, or the commonest error cannot occur.

factStatement: Two sets of values may share a centre and differ entirely in how spread out they are.
familyName: Distinguishing spread from centre
measurementObjective: Given two sets of values, compare their spread or give a stated measure of it.
distractorStrategy: The set with the larger mean assumed to have the larger spread; the count of values taken as spread; the range computed from the wrong pair of values.
notes: Every comparison stem must hold the mean equal between the two sets, which forces the reasoning onto spread.

factStatement: Probabilities add only when events cannot both happen; otherwise the overlap is counted twice.
familyName: Combining the probabilities of two events
measurementObjective: Given two events, give the probability that at least one occurs.
distractorStrategy: The plain sum where the events overlap, sometimes exceeding one, which is the visible symptom; the overlap subtracted where the events are already exclusive; the product offered.
notes: A sum exceeding one is the strongest available stem, since the answer can be rejected without computing the right one.

factStatement: When one event does not affect another, the probability of both is the product; when it does, the product is wrong.
familyName: Deciding whether events multiply
measurementObjective: Given two events, say whether they are independent and give the probability that both occur.
distractorStrategy: A product taken for a draw without replacement, where the second probability has changed; the sum offered; independence assumed from the events being unrelated in subject matter rather than in effect.
notes: Drawing without replacement is the clearest dependent case and every stem should make replacement explicit.

factStatement: A single extreme value can move the mean substantially while leaving the median almost unchanged.
familyName: Diagnosing a summary distorted by an extreme value
measurementObjective: Given a set with an extreme value, say which summary it distorts and by how much it moves.
distractorStrategy: Both summaries claimed to move equally; the median claimed to be the more affected; the effect on the mean stated in the wrong direction.

factStatement: Independent trials have no memory: a run of one outcome changes nothing about the next.
familyName: Diagnosing a claim that past results affect the next trial
measurementObjective: Given a claim about what is now due or more likely, say whether it is warranted.
distractorStrategy: The fallacy stated in its persuasive form — a long run makes the other outcome due; the opposite fallacy, that the run will continue; a correct rejection given for the wrong reason.
notes: One stem should involve a genuinely dependent process, where the same-sounding claim is correct.

conceptName: What a summary does not say
factStatement: Very different sets of values can share a mean, a median, or both, so a summary constrains a distribution without determining it.
familyName: Reasoning about what a summary leaves undetermined
measurementObjective: Given one or two summary values, say what can and cannot be concluded about the underlying values.
distractorStrategy: A conclusion about individual values drawn from the mean — that someone must be near it; equal means taken to imply similar sets; the honest "cannot be determined" offered where the summaries do settle the question.

factStatement: Which summary to report is settled by the question being asked and the shape of the data, not by convention.
familyName: Choosing the summary that answers the question asked
measurementObjective: Given a question and described data, choose the summary that answers it honestly.
distractorStrategy: The mean chosen for visibly skewed data — the default that the family exists to interrogate; the mode chosen where values rarely repeat; a summary of centre offered where the question is about spread.
notes: Every option must be a real summary correctly computed; only its fitness for the stated question separates them.

factStatement: A conclusion drawn from a small or self-selected sample may be true of that sample and say nothing about the wider group.
familyName: Judging what a sample can support
measurementObjective: Given a described sample and a conclusion drawn from it, say whether the conclusion is warranted.
distractorStrategy: A conclusion rejected purely for sample size where the selection is the real fault; one accepted because the arithmetic is correct; a rejection so broad it would rule out all sampling.
notes: Selection bias and sample size must be separable in the stems, since a student who rejects everything small is not reasoning.

factStatement: Machine learning is one way of building artificial intelligence, and deep learning is one way of doing machine learning.
familyName: Placing the three terms inside one another
measurementObjective: Given the three terms, say which contains which.
distractorStrategy: The nesting reversed, with artificial intelligence placed inside machine learning; the three offered as separate fields that do not overlap; deep learning equated with the whole of the subject.
notes: The widest entry point. Keep it about scope rather than about what any of them can do.

factStatement: A rule-based system does what someone wrote down; a learned system does what its examples supported.
familyName: Deciding whether a system was written or trained
measurementObjective: Given a described system, say whether its behaviour was programmed or learned from examples.
distractorStrategy: Any system that behaves cleverly assumed to be learned — a spell checker with a word list is the productive case; a learned system called rule-based because its output is consistent.
notes: At least one stem should be a rule-based system that looks intelligent, since that is where the assumption shows.

factStatement: Training data is the examples a system generalises from; it is not a store the system looks answers up in.
familyName: Recognising what training data does
measurementObjective: Given a description of training, say what the examples were used for.
distractorStrategy: Training data treated as a lookup table the system consults at use time — the single commonest model students hold; examples treated as instructions written by hand.

conceptName: What kind of question is being asked
factStatement: Sorting things into named categories, predicting a number, and grouping without categories are three different tasks.
familyName: Naming the shape of a described task
measurementObjective: Given a task in plain words, say whether it sorts into categories, predicts a quantity, or groups without them.
distractorStrategy: A prediction of a number described as sorting into categories, and the reverse; grouping confused with sorting, which differs only in whether the categories were named in advance.

conceptName: What kind of question is being asked
factStatement: A task where the right answer is recorded for each example is a different problem from one where it is not.
familyName: Deciding whether the examples carry answers
measurementObjective: Given a described collection of data, say whether it already contains the answers a system would learn from.
distractorStrategy: Data assumed to carry answers because it is well organised; answers assumed absent because nobody wrote them deliberately, where past outcomes supply them.
notes: Historical outcomes as accidental answers is the case worth asking about — a record of which customers left is a set of answers nobody set out to create.

conceptName: When learning is the wrong tool
factStatement: A task whose rule is already known and can be written down does not need a system to discover it.
familyName: Deciding whether a task needs learning at all
measurementObjective: Given a task, say whether it calls for a learned system or a written rule.
distractorStrategy: Learning chosen for a task with an exact known rule — computing tax, validating a checksum; a written rule chosen for a task nobody can state, such as recognising a handwritten digit.
notes: Both errors must appear across the family, or it teaches that one answer is always right.

conceptName: What comes out of the examples
factStatement: A system can only pick up distinctions its examples actually contain.
familyName: Reasoning about what a set of examples supports
measurementObjective: Given a described set of examples, say what a system could and could not learn to tell apart.
distractorStrategy: A distinction the examples never contained assumed learnable; a distinction present in the examples denied because it was not the stated purpose.

conceptName: What comes out of the examples
factStatement: Behaviour on inputs unlike anything in the examples is not predictable from performance on inputs like them.
familyName: Predicting behaviour on an unfamiliar input
measurementObjective: Given how a system performed on its examples, say what follows about an input unlike them.
distractorStrategy: Performance assumed to carry over to any input; the system assumed to refuse or to signal doubt, where a confident wrong answer is the usual outcome.
notes: That the system answers confidently rather than declining is the point; a stem should make the unfamiliarity concrete rather than abstract.

factStatement: A high proportion correct can be achieved by ignoring a rare case entirely.
familyName: Reasoning about what an accuracy figure reports
measurementObjective: Given an accuracy figure and the makeup of the data, say what the figure does and does not establish.
distractorStrategy: A 99 per cent figure accepted as strong where 99 per cent of cases share one answer; the figure rejected as meaningless, which overcorrects.
notes: The rare-disease shape is the canonical stem and the arithmetic must stay trivial.

conceptName: What a trained system cannot do
factStatement: A learned system produces an answer; it does not thereby produce a reason, and any reason it states is another output rather than a record of its working.
familyName: Reasoning about what a trained system can be asked for
measurementObjective: Given a request made of a trained system, say whether the system can supply it.
distractorStrategy: A stated reason accepted as the real cause of the answer; the system assumed unable to produce any explanation at all, which is also wrong.

conceptName: When the examples were the problem
factStatement: A group absent from the examples is a group the system was never asked to handle.
familyName: Tracing a failure back to the examples
measurementObjective: Given a system failing on a particular kind of input, decide whether the examples explain it.
distractorStrategy: The method blamed where the data is at fault; more data of the same kind proposed as the fix, which does not close the gap.

conceptName: When the examples were the problem
factStatement: A system will use whatever distinguishes the examples, including something that has nothing to do with the task.
familyName: Identifying a system that learned the wrong thing
measurementObjective: Given a system that scores well and fails in use, identify the incidental signal it used.
distractorStrategy: Insufficient data proposed where the data was plentiful and misleading; the signal named in a way that would also have been present in the failing cases.
notes: The stem must supply the incidental difference, or the item becomes a guess about the world.

factStatement: A system measured on the same examples it learned from reports how well it memorised, not how well it will do.
