familyName: Distinguishing hint text from a real starting value
measurementObjective: Given a field showing text before anything is typed, say what is submitted if it is left alone.
distractorStrategy: The hint assumed to be submitted; a real default assumed to vanish like a hint; both assumed to satisfy a requirement that the field not be empty.
notes: The two look identical before typing, which is what makes this worth an item and a real source of bugs.

conceptName: A field that arrives with nothing
factStatement: A value failing to arrive can mean the control had no name, was disabled, or was never chosen — and the three need different fixes.
familyName: Diagnosing a field that submits nothing
measurementObjective: Given a value absent from a submission, identify which cause fits the described form.
distractorStrategy: A cause named that the described fragment rules out; the server blamed where the form is at fault; a cause that would have produced an empty value rather than an absent one.

conceptName: A field that arrives with nothing
factStatement: Controls that appear together and do not share a name behave independently, so several can be chosen at once.
familyName: Diagnosing controls that should exclude one another and do not
measurementObjective: Given options that can all be chosen at once, identify why.
distractorStrategy: The kind of control blamed rather than the naming; the layout blamed; a fix proposed that changes appearance without changing grouping.

conceptName: What checking in the browser guarantees
factStatement: Validation in the browser helps the person filling the form and guarantees nothing about what arrives at the server.
familyName: Reasoning about what browser validation establishes
measurementObjective: Given a form validated in the browser, say what the server may still receive.
distractorStrategy: The check treated as a guarantee; the check dismissed as pointless, which throws away its real purpose; the risk described as requiring unusual expertise.
notes: Both the over-trust and the over-correction must be available, since a student who removes browser validation has also missed the point.

conceptName: Choosing what the form should contain
factStatement: How many answers are allowed, whether the set is fixed, and whether an answer is optional decide which controls a requirement needs.
familyName: Choosing controls that meet a stated requirement
measurementObjective: Given a requirement, choose the arrangement of controls that satisfies it exactly.
distractorStrategy: An arrangement permitting several answers where one is required; one forcing an answer the requirement says is optional; one that is usable and cannot express a stated case.

conceptName: Choosing what the form should contain
factStatement: What identifies each value, which controls contribute one, and what happens when a field is left alone are the questions to ask of any form.
familyName: Reasoning about an unfamiliar form from its description
measurementObjective: Given a form built with an unfamiliar toolkit, say what a described submission contains.
distractorStrategy: An answer assuming every control contributes; one assuming an untouched field sends its hint; one requiring behaviour the description does not grant.
notes: The toolkit is described in the stem and never named, so this measures the model rather than familiarity.

factStatement: A barrier is identified by naming who cannot do what, rather than by whether a page looks acceptable.
familyName: Saying who a described barrier affects
measurementObjective: Given a described page fault, say who is prevented from doing what.
distractorStrategy: Every barrier attributed to blindness, where keyboard use, low vision and colour vision are separate; the barrier described as inconvenience rather than prevention.
notes: The range of who is affected is the point; a skill that only ever means screen readers measures one quarter of the subject.

factStatement: An image carrying information needs a description; one that is purely decorative should be passed over silently rather than described.
familyName: Deciding whether an image needs describing at all
measurementObjective: Given an image and its role on the page, say whether it should be described or ignored.
distractorStrategy: Every image assumed to need a description, which makes decorative images noise; a meaningful image passed over because it also looks decorative; the file name offered as a description.
notes: This is deliberately about whether to describe rather than what to write, which is where the banked HTML family sits.

factStatement: Anything that can be clicked must also be reachable and operable by keyboard, and elements made clickable by script often are not.
familyName: Deciding whether a described control can be reached by keyboard
measurementObjective: Given a described control, say whether a keyboard user can operate it.
distractorStrategy: A clickable region assumed reachable because it responds to a click; reachability judged by whether the control is visible; a genuine control assumed unreachable because it is styled unusually.

conceptName: What the shape of a page says
factStatement: Heading levels state how sections nest, and are used to move around a page by people who cannot see its layout.
familyName: Reading what a sequence of heading levels claims
measurementObjective: Given a sequence of heading levels, say what structure it describes.
distractorStrategy: Levels read as sizes rather than as nesting; a skipped level treated as harmless; the structure read from visual grouping rather than from the levels.

factStatement: A control with no accessible name is announced by its kind alone, which tells the user a button exists and not what it does.
familyName: Recognising a control that would announce nothing useful
measurementObjective: Given a described control, say what a non-visual user would learn about it.
distractorStrategy: An icon-only control assumed to be named by its icon; nearby text assumed to supply the name; the control assumed unusable rather than usable and unidentifiable.
notes: Icon-only buttons are the case, and they look perfectly finished to a sighted reviewer.

factStatement: Keyboard focus moves through controls in the order they appear in the markup, which need not be the order they appear on screen.
familyName: Working out the order the keyboard visits controls in
measurementObjective: Given a described page whose visual and markup orders differ, say the order focus follows.
distractorStrategy: The visual order given, which is the whole trap; the order reversed; focus assumed to skip anything not currently visible.
notes: Both orders are stated in the stem, so the answer is derivable rather than a guess about how a browser behaves.

factStatement: Information conveyed only by colour is unavailable to anyone who cannot distinguish those colours, and to anyone hearing the page read aloud.
familyName: Identifying information carried only by colour
measurementObjective: Given a described interface, say what information is lost if colour cannot be seen.
distractorStrategy: Colour used redundantly alongside text flagged as a fault, which it is not; the fault described as one of taste; a remedy proposed that changes the colours rather than adding a second channel.
notes: Redundant colour must appear as a non-fault, or the family teaches that colour is forbidden.

conceptName: Text that has to stand alone
factStatement: Links are frequently listed on their own, so link text has to say where it goes without the sentence around it.
familyName: Judging whether link text works on its own
measurementObjective: Given link text, say whether its destination is clear without the surrounding sentence.
distractorStrategy: Text judged in its sentence rather than alone; a long link text assumed better; the address itself offered as good link text.

factStatement: An error shown only as a colour or only beside a field may never reach a user who is not looking at that part of the screen.
familyName: Deciding whether an error message would reach the user
measurementObjective: Given a described error presentation, say whether a non-visual user learns what is wrong.
distractorStrategy: A visible message assumed to be announced; the message assumed to be found because it is on the page; a remedy that makes the message louder visually.

factStatement: The same image needs a different description, or none, depending on what it is doing on the page.
familyName: Deciding what to announce for an image in a stated role
measurementObjective: Given one image in two different roles, say how the description should differ.
distractorStrategy: The same description used for both roles; an image inside a link described by its appearance rather than by where the link goes; the description written for a sighted reader.
notes: An image that is the whole of a link is the discriminating role and is where the banked family stops.

factStatement: A control that works perfectly with a mouse can be impossible to reach any other way, and nothing about the page looks wrong.
familyName: Diagnosing a control that cannot be reached
measurementObjective: Given a control that keyboard users cannot operate, identify why.
distractorStrategy: Styling blamed rather than the kind of element; the fault attributed to the browser; a remedy proposed that makes it visible rather than reachable.

factStatement: Markup chosen for how it looks tells anything reading the structure something untrue about the page.
familyName: Diagnosing structure that misdescribes the page
measurementObjective: Given a page whose structure misleads, identify what it claims that is untrue.
distractorStrategy: A visual fault named instead of a structural claim; the false claim stated about the wrong element; the fault dismissed because the page reads correctly on screen.

conceptName: Whether two people learn the same thing
factStatement: The test is whether two users can learn the same things and do the same things, not whether their experience is the same.
familyName: Judging whether two users get the same information
measurementObjective: Given a page and two described users, say whether both can obtain the same information.
distractorStrategy: A difference in experience treated as a failure of equivalence; a genuine loss of information dismissed because a workaround exists; equivalence claimed where one user must ask for help.
notes: A workaround that requires another person is not equivalence, and that distinction is the item.

factStatement: A change that improves a page generally may leave the specific barrier exactly where it was.
familyName: Choosing the fix that removes the stated barrier
measurementObjective: Given a barrier and several proposed changes, choose the one that removes it.
distractorStrategy: A genuine improvement that addresses a different barrier; a change that hides the symptom; a remedy that helps one group and creates a barrier for another.
notes: Every option must be a real improvement, so only relevance to the stated barrier separates them.

factStatement: Asking who cannot reach it, who cannot perceive it and who is not told what happened works on any interface, not only a web page.
familyName: Applying the reasoning to an unfamiliar interface
measurementObjective: Given an interface that is not a web page, identify the barrier in it.
distractorStrategy: A web-specific remedy proposed for a non-web interface; a barrier named that the description rules out; a general complaint about the design offered as a barrier.
notes: Kiosks, printed forms and voice menus are all fair ground and none of them has markup.

factStatement: Finding where something is defined, finding everywhere it is used, and finding text that looks like it are three different questions with three different answers.
familyName: Matching a question to the feature that answers it
measurementObjective: Given something a developer needs to know, say which kind of feature answers it.
distractorStrategy: Plain text search offered where a question about meaning is asked; a definition lookup offered where every usage is wanted; the two directions of the question exchanged.
notes: Features are described by what they answer and never named, so nothing here dates with a release.

factStatement: A search reports what it found within what it looked at, and what it looked at may exclude whole directories.
familyName: Saying what a search actually covered
measurementObjective: Given a search and its stated scope, say what an empty result establishes.
distractorStrategy: No results read as proof of absence from the project; excluded directories assumed to have been searched; the scope assumed to include files not open.
notes: An empty result meaning nothing is the point, and it is how people conclude a symbol is unused.

conceptName: What a marker is telling you
factStatement: An underline or a marker is one tool's opinion about the code, and different tools produce different opinions about the same line.
familyName: Saying what a marker in the editor claims
measurementObjective: Given a described marker, say what it asserts about the code.
distractorStrategy: A style warning read as an error; an error read as a style preference; the marker assumed to come from actually running the code.

factStatement: Following a name takes you to where the tool has worked out it is defined, which can be wrong when the same name exists in several places.
familyName: Reasoning about where following a name leads
measurementObjective: Given a name defined in more than one place, say where following it would lead and how to be sure.
distractorStrategy: The answer assumed unique where the stem gives two definitions; the tool assumed to offer a choice always; the first alphabetically assumed.

factStatement: A search for usages finds the places the tool can see, and misses names built up as text or reached indirectly.
familyName: Judging whether a usage search found everything
measurementObjective: Given a usage search and a described codebase, say what it would have missed.
distractorStrategy: The result treated as complete; the tool assumed to find a name assembled at run time; completeness assumed to depend on the size of the project.

factStatement: Renaming through the tool changes what it recognised as the same thing, and leaves untouched anything it could not see.
familyName: Working out what a rename would and would not change
measurementObjective: Given a described codebase, say what a rename touches and what is left behind.
distractorStrategy: Occurrences in comments and text assumed to be updated; a same-named but unrelated symbol assumed to be changed too; the rename assumed to reach a configuration file.
notes: A name appearing in a configuration file or a template is the case that breaks after a clean rename.

factStatement: A terminal opened inside an editor starts in a particular directory, which is often the project root rather than the folder of the open file.
familyName: Reasoning about where a built-in terminal is running
measurementObjective: Given a project and an open file, say where a command typed in the terminal would act.
distractorStrategy: The directory of the open file assumed; the location assumed to follow the file as it changes; the home directory assumed.
notes: This is why a relative path that works in the terminal fails when the same command is run elsewhere.

factStatement: Pressing run hands the code to an interpreter or compiler chosen by a setting, and several may be installed.
familyName: Reasoning about what will execute the code
measurementObjective: Given a machine with several environments installed, say what decides which one runs.
distractorStrategy: The editor assumed to run the code itself; the newest installed version assumed; the choice assumed to follow the file rather than a setting.

conceptName: What a marker is telling you
factStatement: Code the editor marks may run perfectly, and code the editor accepts may fail immediately.
familyName: Separating what the editor says from what happens
measurementObjective: Given a marker and a described outcome, say what each establishes.
distractorStrategy: A marked line assumed to be why the program failed; a clean file assumed to be correct; the marker assumed to update after the program runs.

factStatement: An extension gives the editor knowledge of a language; it does not install the tools that compile or run it.
familyName: Saying what installing an extension does and does not provide
measurementObjective: Given an installed extension, say what has and has not become possible.
distractorStrategy: The extension assumed to install the language; assumed to do nothing beyond colouring the text; the absence of markers after installing read as the code being correct.

conceptName: When the tool is out of date
factStatement: A tool that has not re-examined the project reports what was true when it last looked.
familyName: Diagnosing a warning that no longer applies
measurementObjective: Given a marker that contradicts the code, decide whether it is out of date and what to do.
distractorStrategy: The code changed to satisfy a marker that is simply stale; the tool assumed always current; every inconvenient marker dismissed as stale, which is the mirrored error.
notes: Both errors must appear across the family — editing correct code to silence a stale warning is the expensive one.

conceptName: When the tool is out of date
factStatement: Code run by a different environment from the one it was prepared for fails in ways that look like faults in the code.
familyName: Diagnosing code run by the wrong environment
measurementObjective: Given a failure that does not match the code, decide whether the environment explains it.
distractorStrategy: The code blamed for a missing library that is installed elsewhere; the library assumed uninstalled; a version difference proposed where the stem shows a different environment entirely.
notes: A package that is installed and not found is the signature, and it is the commonest first-year environment fault.

factStatement: A tool reporting nothing means it found nothing it checks for, which is a much narrower claim than the code being correct.
familyName: Reasoning about what a tool reporting nothing establishes
measurementObjective: Given a clean report from a described tool, say what it supports and what it leaves open.
distractorStrategy: Silence read as correctness; the tool dismissed as worthless; a conclusion drawn about a property the tool never examines, such as whether the logic is right.

factStatement: Which feature answers a question soonest depends on whether the question is about meaning, about text, or about what actually happens.
familyName: Choosing the quickest reliable way to answer a question
measurementObjective: Given a question about a codebase, choose the approach that answers it reliably.
distractorStrategy: A text search chosen for a question about meaning; a feature chosen that answers a neighbouring question; reading the whole file, which works and is the slowest.
notes: Every option must eventually work; only reliability and cost separate them.

factStatement: What did this search cover, what did this change reach, and what is this marker claiming are the questions to ask of any tool.
familyName: Reasoning about an unfamiliar editor from what it claims to do
measurementObjective: Given an unfamiliar tool described by its stated behaviour, say what its report establishes.
distractorStrategy: A capability assumed that the description does not grant; the report read as covering more than the stated scope; the tool distrusted entirely despite a clear statement of what it checks.
notes: The tool is described in the stem and never named, so this measures the reasoning rather than product familiarity.

conceptName: Ways of writing text in a program
factStatement: Text can be written between single or double quotes, and the two behave identically except in which quote they may contain.
familyName: Recognising the forms a written piece of text may take
measurementObjective: Given several written forms, say which are valid and equivalent.
distractorStrategy: The two quote forms assumed to differ in meaning; mismatched opening and closing quotes accepted; a form assumed invalid because it is less common.
notes: This skill is literals and formatting throughout. Indexing, slicing and searching belong to the banked text skill and appear nowhere here.

factStatement: A backslash and the character after it stand together for one character, which is often not either of the two written.
familyName: Saying what an escaped pair stands for
measurementObjective: Given a written escape, say which single character it produces.
distractorStrategy: The pair read as two characters; the backslash read as itself with the letter as itself; an escape assumed to be a formatting instruction rather than a character.

conceptName: Text with values placed into it
factStatement: A literal marked for interpolation replaces the marked sections with the values they name; an unmarked one contains the braces as text.
familyName: Recognising a literal that substitutes values
measurementObjective: Given two similar literals, say which substitutes and which does not.
distractorStrategy: Braces assumed always to substitute; the marker assumed to be needed only when a value is present; substitution assumed to work in a literal built by joining.
notes: The unmarked literal producing braces verbatim is the observable difference and should decide the stems.

conceptName: Text with values placed into it
factStatement: A substituted value is converted to text, so a number appears without quotes and a collection appears in its written form.
familyName: Working out what an interpolating literal produces
measurementObjective: Given a literal and the values of its names, give the text produced.
distractorStrategy: The name reproduced instead of its value; quotes added around a substituted number; the surrounding text dropped.

factStatement: A literal marked raw treats every backslash as a backslash, which is why it suits paths and patterns.
familyName: Saying what marking a literal raw changes
measurementObjective: Given the same text written raw and not, say how the two differ.
distractorStrategy: Raw assumed to change how the text is displayed rather than what it contains; raw assumed to disable interpolation as well; the two forms assumed identical for text with no backslash, which is true and not what was asked.

factStatement: A literal written between triple quotes contains every line break and every leading space exactly as typed.
familyName: Working out what a multi-line literal contains
measurementObjective: Given a triple-quoted literal as written, say what it contains.
distractorStrategy: Indentation assumed to be stripped — the error that produces mysteriously misaligned output; the line break after the opening quotes overlooked; line breaks assumed to become spaces.
notes: The literal is shown with its indentation explicit in the stem, since that is the whole of the measurement.

factStatement: A substituted value can be given a width or a number of decimal places, which changes only how it is written out.
familyName: Working out what a width or precision produces
measurementObjective: Given a value and a stated format, give the text produced.
distractorStrategy: A width assumed to truncate rather than pad; a precision assumed to truncate where it rounds; padding applied on the wrong side.
notes: Padding and truncation are opposite behaviours and are the pair worth separating here.

factStatement: Adding two pieces of text joins them and multiplying text by a whole number repeats it; neither does anything arithmetic.
familyName: Working out what an operator applied to text produces
measurementObjective: Given text combined with an operator, give the result.
distractorStrategy: Text that looks numeric assumed to be added arithmetically; repetition assumed to insert a separator; the result of combining text with a number assumed to work.
notes: Two pieces of text that look like numbers is the discriminating stem.

factStatement: Two written pieces of text placed next to each other with nothing between them become one, which is useful deliberately and dangerous by accident.
familyName: Predicting what adjacent written literals produce
measurementObjective: Given two literals written next to each other, say what results.
distractorStrategy: A separator assumed to be inserted; an error assumed; in a list with a missing comma, the two assumed to remain separate items.
notes: A list with a comma left out is the accidental case and produces a list one item shorter than intended.

conceptName: Text with values placed into it
factStatement: A value of any kind placed into a literal is converted to its written form, which for a collection includes its brackets and separators.
familyName: Working out what a non-text value produces when substituted
measurementObjective: Given a collection or an absent value substituted into a literal, give the resulting text.
distractorStrategy: A collection assumed to be flattened into its elements; an absent value assumed to produce nothing rather than a word; brackets assumed to be omitted.
notes: An absent value appearing in output as a word is a real and confusing result and belongs here.

factStatement: A quote of the same kind as the one that opened a literal ends it there, and everything after it is read as something else.
familyName: Diagnosing a literal broken by its own quote
measurementObjective: Given a literal that fails, identify where it actually ended and how to fix it.
distractorStrategy: The whole line reported as invalid without locating the end; a fix proposed that removes the apostrophe rather than the clash; the fault attributed to the length of the text.
notes: Two fixes exist — the other quote form, or an escape — and a good stem makes both available.

factStatement: A backslash followed by certain letters becomes a different character, so a path written plainly may not contain what was typed.
familyName: Diagnosing text mangled by an unintended escape
measurementObjective: Given a path that behaves wrongly, identify which part was transformed.
distractorStrategy: The whole path assumed transformed rather than one pair; the file assumed missing; a fix proposed that changes the separator without addressing the escape.
notes: Only some letters form an escape, so a path can be right in one place and wrong in another — that unevenness is the item.

factStatement: Rounding a value for display leaves the value itself untouched, so later arithmetic uses the original.
familyName: Reasoning about what formatting for display affects
measurementObjective: Given a value formatted for display and then used again, say what the later use works with.
distractorStrategy: The value assumed to have been rounded permanently; the displayed total assumed to equal the sum of the displayed parts; the discrepancy attributed to a fault.
notes: Displayed figures that do not add up to the displayed total is the consequence, and it is a genuine reporting problem.

factStatement: Which literal form to use is settled by what the text contains — quotes, backslashes, line breaks — rather than by preference.
familyName: Choosing the literal form for stated content
measurementObjective: Given text with awkward characters in it, choose the form that expresses it without escapes.
distractorStrategy: A form chosen that requires escaping the very character the alternative would have avoided; a raw form chosen for text that must end in a backslash, which raw literals cannot express; a form chosen for brevity.
notes: Text ending in a backslash is the case where the obvious form genuinely fails and is worth one item.

factStatement: Quote forms, escapes, raw text and substitution appear across languages with different spellings and the same behaviour.
familyName: Reasoning about literals in an unfamiliar language
measurementObjective: Given an unfamiliar language's rules for literals, say what a written literal contains.
distractorStrategy: Python behaviour assumed where the stated rules differ; substitution assumed available where the rules do not mention it; an escape assumed to work in a form the rules describe as raw.
notes: The rules are stated in the stem and the language is invented, so this measures reading the rules rather than knowing a second language.
